explanation: This idea is used to explain why weight loss stalls. The slowdown is real but modest, and stalls are often due to eating more than people realise or being less active. Very low intakes are still unwise without medical supervision because of nutrient shortfalls and muscle loss.

myth: Eating too much sugar directly causes diabetes.
fact: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition and is not caused by sugar or diet. Type 2 diabetes is linked to excess weight, inactivity, age and family history; sugary drinks and foods can contribute through weight gain, and sugary drinks in particular are linked to higher risk.
explanation: Because diabetes involves high blood sugar, it seems logical that eating sugar causes it. The relationship is indirect: a diet high in calories from any source, including sugar, raises the risk of type 2 diabetes. Cutting down on sugary drinks is still a sensible step.

myth: Echinacea reliably prevents and cures colds.
fact: Research on echinacea for colds has produced mixed results. Some studies suggest a small benefit in preventing colds, but there is no strong evidence that it cures them or shortens them substantially.
explanation: Echinacea products vary widely in the plant species, parts used and preparation, which makes results hard to compare. It may cause allergic reactions, especially in people allergic to plants in the daisy family. Rest, fluids and time remain the mainstays of cold care.

myth: Eczema and psoriasis are contagious.
fact: Eczema and psoriasis cannot be caught from another person. They are related to the immune system, genetics and skin barrier, not infection.
explanation: Visible rashes can lead to stigma, which affects quality of life. Eczema skin can sometimes become infected, and that infection may need treatment, but the condition itself does not spread.

myth: Educational videos and apps help babies learn to talk faster.
fact: Babies and toddlers learn language mainly through live, back-and-forth interaction with people, such as talking, reading and playing together. The WHO recommends no sedentary screen time for children under 2.
explanation: Studies have found that very young children learn far less from screens than from real conversation. Occasional video calls with family are different, because they involve real interaction. Reading aloud, singing and talking about what you are doing all help language develop.

sources.label: WHO — To grow up healthy, children need to sit less and play more

myth: Eggs are bad for your heart because of their cholesterol.
fact: For most people, cholesterol in food has a smaller effect on blood cholesterol than saturated and trans fats do. Eggs can be part of a healthy, balanced diet, although people with certain conditions may be advised to limit them.
explanation: Egg yolks are high in dietary cholesterol, which is why eggs were long seen as a heart risk. Research suggests moderate egg eating is not strongly linked to heart disease in healthy people, though findings vary and some people respond more strongly. How eggs are cooked and served, such as with bacon, sausages or butter, often matters more than the eggs.

myth: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a barbaric treatment that fries your brain.
fact: Modern ECT is given under general anaesthetic with a muscle relaxant and is used mainly for severe depression and some other serious conditions when other treatments have not worked or rapid help is needed. It is one of the most effective treatments for severe depression.
explanation: Its image comes partly from older practices and films. ECT does have side effects, most notably short-term confusion and memory problems, and some people report longer-lasting memory gaps, so its risks and benefits need careful discussion. It is only given with consent, except in specific legal circumstances.

myth: Erectile dysfunction can be an early warning sign of heart disease.
fact: Erectile dysfunction is often caused by reduced blood flow, and it can appear before other signs of narrowed arteries. Doctors may check blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar.
explanation: Not everyone with ED has heart disease, and there are many other causes. It is a good reason to have a health check rather than a cause for alarm.

myth: Erectile dysfunction is just a normal part of getting old that you have to accept.
fact: Erectile dysfunction becomes more common with age, but it is not inevitable and it is often treatable at any age.
explanation: Causes include reduced blood flow, diabetes, medicines, stress and relationship issues. Treatments include lifestyle changes, medicines and talking therapies, so it is worth speaking to a doctor.

myth: Everyone has hidden parasites and should do a parasite cleanse.
fact: Most people in countries with clean water and sanitation do not have intestinal parasites. Real parasite infections are diagnosed with tests, such as stool samples, and treated with specific medicines, not general 'cleanse' kits.
explanation: Social media videos often show strands of gut lining, mucus or undigested food passed after a cleanse and claim they are worms. Herbal parasite cleanses are not proven to work and some can cause side effects or interact with medicines. If you think you or your child has worms, such as itching around the bottom at night, a pharmacist or doctor can advise on proper treatment.

myth: Everyone is a little bit autistic.
fact: Many people share some traits seen in autism, such as liking routine or finding loud places tiring. Autism is diagnosed when differences in social communication and repetitive behaviours or sensory sensitivities are present from early childhood and have a significant effect on daily life.
explanation: The phrase is often meant kindly, but it can downplay the real challenges autistic people face. Autism is a lifelong difference in how people experience the world, not a scale everyone sits on. Anyone who thinks they may be autistic can ask a GP about an assessment.

myth: Everyone must drink exactly eight glasses of water a day.
fact: Fluid needs vary with body size, activity, climate and health. Guidance such as the NHS's suggestion of 6 to 8 glasses of fluid a day is a rough guide, and all drinks, including tea, coffee and milk, plus water in food, count towards it.
explanation: The 'eight glasses' rule is easy to remember but was never a strict scientific requirement. Thirst and pale yellow urine are useful guides for most healthy people. Some people, such as those with certain heart or kidney conditions, may be told to limit fluids.

myth: Everyone over 50 should take a daily aspirin to prevent heart attacks.
fact: Low-dose aspirin is recommended for many people who have already had a heart attack or stroke. For people without heart disease, current guidance generally advises against routine daily aspirin because the bleeding risk can outweigh the benefit.
explanation: Advice on aspirin has changed as newer trials showed smaller benefits and real risks of stomach and brain bleeding. Whether aspirin is right depends on your personal risk. Do not start or stop daily aspirin without speaking to a doctor.

myth: Exercise will wear out arthritic joints faster.
fact: Regular, appropriate exercise is one of the main treatments for osteoarthritis. It reduces pain, improves function and strengthens muscles that support the joints.
explanation: Low-impact activities such as walking, swimming and cycling, plus strengthening exercises, are often recommended. A physiotherapist can tailor a plan, and some discomfort while starting is normal.

myth: Eye exercises can cure short-sightedness so you don't need glasses.
fact: Eye exercises cannot correct refractive errors such as short-sightedness, long-sightedness or astigmatism, which are due to the shape of the eye.
explanation: Some specific exercises are used for certain eye-muscle or focusing problems under specialist supervision. Glasses, contact lenses and laser surgery are the proven ways to correct refractive errors.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Fat around your waist is more harmful to health than fat elsewhere on your body.
fact: Fat stored deep around the abdominal organs (visceral fat) is more strongly linked to type 2 diabetes, heart disease and some other conditions than fat on the hips or thighs. That is why waist size is used alongside BMI to judge health risk.
explanation: You can carry extra visceral fat even if your weight is in the 'healthy' BMI range. A simple check is your waist measurement: as a general guide, your waist should be less than half your height. Regular activity, a balanced diet, enough sleep and limiting alcohol all help reduce visceral fat; sit-ups alone do not target it.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — Taking aim at belly fat

myth: Fat-burning pills and slimming teas help you lose weight safely.
fact: There is little good evidence that over-the-counter weight-loss supplements or slimming teas lead to meaningful, lasting weight loss. Some have been found to contain hidden drugs or ingredients that can cause serious harm.
explanation: These products are heavily advertised on social media, often with before-and-after photos. Many slimming teas act as laxatives, so any quick weight drop is mostly water, not fat. Products containing stimulants can raise blood pressure and heart rate.

sources.label: NIH ODS — Dietary supplements for weight loss

myth: Feed a cold, starve a fever.
fact: There is no evidence that eating more helps a cold or that going without food helps a fever. With either illness, the main advice is to rest, drink plenty of fluids and eat as your appetite allows.
explanation: This saying is centuries old and was based on ideas about body heat rather than evidence. A fever increases fluid loss, so staying hydrated matters more than food. Not feeling hungry when unwell is normal, but avoiding food deliberately is not helpful.
keywords: should i eat with a fever

myth: Feeling depressed is just part of getting old.
fact: Depression is not a normal part of ageing. It is treatable at any age, and older adults respond to treatment much like younger people.
explanation: Loss, illness and isolation can raise the risk, and depression in older people is often missed or mistaken for physical illness or dementia. If you or someone you know is struggling, talking to a doctor is a good first step; anyone in crisis should get urgent help.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Fertility falls off a cliff on your 35th birthday.
fact: Female fertility declines gradually with age, faster after about 35, but there is no sudden drop on a particular birthday. Many people conceive naturally after 35.
explanation: Age does increase the time to conceive and the risk of miscarriage and some complications. People over 35 are often advised to seek help sooner if they have not conceived after six months of trying.

myth: Fish oil capsules prevent heart attacks.
fact: Most large trials have found that standard fish oil supplements do not prevent heart attacks or strokes in the general population. Eating oily fish as part of a healthy diet is linked to better heart health, and some prescription omega-3 medicines are used for specific people with high triglycerides.
explanation: The link between fish-eating populations and lower heart disease led to supplement popularity. Some studies have linked omega-3 supplements to a higher risk of atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm. Speak to a doctor if you are considering omega-3 for a heart condition.

myth: Flat cola or sports drinks are the best treatment for diarrhoea and vomiting.
fact: Fizzy drinks and fruit juices contain a lot of sugar and too little salt, and can make diarrhoea worse, especially in children. Oral rehydration solutions are designed to replace lost fluid and salts and are recommended for people at risk of dehydration.
explanation: Flat cola is a common home remedy, and for a healthy adult with mild illness small sips of any fluid are better than none. Babies and young children are at higher risk of dehydration and should keep feeding, with oral rehydration solution if advised. Seek help for signs of dehydration such as very little urine, drowsiness or a dry mouth.

myth: Flossing is pointless.
fact: The research evidence for flossing specifically is limited, but cleaning between the teeth with floss or interdental brushes is still recommended because a toothbrush cannot reach those surfaces.
explanation: Headlines about weak flossing studies led some people to stop. Many dentists find interdental brushes easier and effective. Ask your dentist which method suits you.

myth: Flu is just a bad cold.
fact: Flu is caused by different viruses from the common cold and is usually more severe, often with sudden fever, body aches and exhaustion. Seasonal flu causes hundreds of thousands of deaths worldwide each year, according to WHO.
explanation: People often say they have 'flu' when they have a heavy cold, which makes real flu seem mild. Flu can lead to pneumonia and is especially dangerous for older people, young children, pregnant people and those with long-term conditions. Annual vaccination reduces the risk.

myth: Fluoride toothpaste is harmful and should be avoided.
fact: Fluoride toothpaste is one of the most effective ways to prevent tooth decay and is safe when used as directed.
explanation: Children should use the right amount for their age (a smear or pea-sized amount) and be supervised so they spit rather than swallow. Too much fluoride in early childhood can cause harmless white marks on teeth.

myth: Flying is dangerous for your unborn baby.
fact: For most people with a straightforward pregnancy, flying is not harmful to the baby. Airlines may have rules about travelling late in pregnancy, often from around 37 weeks (earlier for twins), and may ask for a letter from your midwife or doctor after about 28 weeks.
explanation: Long flights raise the risk of blood clots (DVT), so drink water, move around and consider compression stockings. Check your travel insurance covers pregnancy and that you can get care at your destination. If you have complications, ask your midwife or doctor before booking.

myth: Food dropped on the floor is safe to eat if you pick it up within five seconds.
fact: Bacteria can transfer to food the moment it touches a contaminated surface. Moist foods and dirty surfaces pick up more bacteria, and longer contact increases transfer, but there is no safe time window.
explanation: The 'five-second rule' is a popular joke that many people take seriously. For most healthy people, eating a dry biscuit off a clean floor is unlikely to cause harm, but the risk depends on the surface, not the speed. Be more careful with food for babies, older people, pregnant people and anyone with a weakened immune system.

myth: Forgetting things, like where you put your keys, means you're getting dementia.
fact: Occasional forgetfulness is common at any age and is not usually a sign of dementia. Stress, tiredness, low mood and busy lives often affect memory.
explanation: Signs that need checking include memory problems that are getting worse and affecting daily life, getting lost in familiar places, or difficulty following conversations. Some causes of memory problems, such as vitamin deficiencies or thyroid problems, are treatable.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Frozen fruit and vegetables are much less nutritious than fresh.
fact: Frozen fruit and vegetables are usually frozen soon after picking, which preserves most of their nutrients. They can be just as nutritious as fresh produce, and sometimes more so than fresh produce that has been stored for days.
explanation: Fresh food feels more natural, so frozen options are often seen as second best. Frozen, canned (in water or juice) and dried fruit and vegetables all count towards daily fruit and vegetable intake. Check labels on frozen products for added salt, sugar or sauces.

myth: Fruit is unhealthy because it is full of sugar.
fact: The sugar in whole fruit comes packaged with fibre, water, vitamins and minerals, and eating whole fruit is linked to better health. WHO's advice to limit free sugars does not apply to sugar naturally present in whole fruit.
explanation: Low-sugar and low-carb trends have led some people to cut out fruit. Fruit juices and smoothies are different, because blending and juicing release the sugars, so health bodies suggest limiting them. Whole fruit is a better snack than most processed sweet foods.

myth: Fruit juice is a healthy everyday drink for babies and toddlers.
fact: Fruit juice contains free sugars that can cause tooth decay, and it is not needed in a young child's diet. Babies under 12 months do not need juice at all; for older children, water and milk are the best everyday drinks.
explanation: If juice is given to older children, health services suggest keeping it small, well diluted and with meals, which reduces harm to teeth. Whole fruit is better than juice because it contains fibre and is more filling. Avoid giving juice in bottles or at bedtime.

sources.label: NHS — Drinks and cups for babies and young children

myth: Garlic or beetroot juice can replace blood pressure medicine.
fact: Some studies suggest garlic supplements or beetroot juice may lower blood pressure slightly, but the effects are small and not a substitute for prescribed medication. Stopping treatment in favour of them can be dangerous.
explanation: Natural remedies appeal to people who want to avoid tablets. Lifestyle changes such as reducing salt, losing weight if needed, exercising and limiting alcohol can make a real difference alongside medicine. Garlic supplements can interact with blood thinners.

myth: Generic medicines are weaker or less effective than brand-name ones.
fact: Generic medicines contain the same active ingredient and must meet the same standards for quality, strength and effect as the brand-name version. They are cheaper mainly because the makers did not have to repeat the original development trials.
explanation: Different colours, shapes or packaging can make generics seem like a different medicine. Inactive ingredients such as fillers may differ, which rarely matters but can be relevant for people with specific allergies. A pharmacist can answer questions about any switch.

myth: Getting a base tan protects you from sunburn.
fact: A tan is a sign of skin damage. It offers very little protection, roughly equivalent to a very low SPF, and does not prevent skin cancer.
explanation: Building a tan before a holiday still exposes skin to harmful UV. Shade, clothing, hats and broad-spectrum sunscreen are recommended instead.

myth: Ginger can help settle nausea.
fact: Research suggests ginger may help ease some types of nausea, including pregnancy-related nausea, though results are mixed and effects are usually modest. It is generally considered safe in food amounts.
explanation: Ginger tea, biscuits or sweets are a reasonable thing to try for mild nausea. High-dose ginger supplements may interact with blood-thinning medicines, so check with a pharmacist if you take other medicines. Vomiting that won't stop, or signs of dehydration, needs medical advice.

myth: Giving babies peanut foods early can lower their chance of developing peanut allergy.
fact: Research, including a large trial known as LEAP, found that introducing peanut-containing foods in infancy greatly reduced peanut allergy in high-risk babies. Guidelines now recommend introducing peanut, in a safe form such as smooth peanut butter mixed into food, around the time solids are started.
explanation: Parents were once advised to delay peanuts, so many people find this surprising. Whole nuts should never be given to young children because of choking risk. Babies with severe eczema or an existing food allergy may need medical advice before peanut is introduced.

myth: Giving babies several vaccines at once overloads their immune system.
fact: A baby's immune system meets huge numbers of germs every day from feeding, touching and breathing. The antigens in the full childhood vaccine schedule are a tiny fraction of what the immune system handles routinely, and combined vaccines are tested for safety together.
explanation: Parents understandably worry when a small baby receives several injections in one visit. Modern vaccines also contain far fewer antigens than older ones did, because they are more purified. Spacing out vaccines does not make them safer but does leave the child unprotected for longer.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: Giving children ADHD medicine turns them into drug addicts later in life.
fact: When ADHD stimulant medicines are prescribed and monitored by doctors, research has not shown that they make children more likely to misuse drugs later. Untreated ADHD itself is linked to a higher risk of substance problems.
explanation: ADHD medicines can have side effects, such as reduced appetite and sleep problems, so they are reviewed regularly. They are one part of treatment, alongside support at home and school. Families with concerns should discuss them with the prescribing doctor rather than stopping medicine suddenly.

sources.label: NHS — ADHD in children and young people

myth: Going outside with wet hair will give you a cold.
fact: Wet hair does not cause colds; only cold viruses do. You may feel chilly and uncomfortable, but you cannot catch a cold without coming into contact with a virus.
explanation: This is a common warning passed down in families. The timing often seems to fit because people catch viruses from others around the same time. Drying your hair in cold weather is still sensible for comfort.

myth: Gout is just caused by eating too much rich food and drinking.
fact: Gout is caused by high levels of uric acid in the blood. Diet and alcohol can trigger attacks, but genetics, kidney function, some medicines and other health conditions are major factors.
explanation: Many people with gout have healthy diets. Long-term medicines that lower uric acid are effective, and lifestyle changes help alongside them.

myth: Green or yellow snot means you have a bacterial infection and need antibiotics.
fact: Mucus often turns yellow or green during ordinary viral colds because of immune cells fighting the infection. The colour alone does not mean you have a bacterial infection or need antibiotics.
explanation: Many people expect antibiotics when their mucus changes colour, and this is a common reason for unnecessary prescriptions. Most colds and sinus infections get better on their own within one to three weeks. See a doctor if symptoms last more than about 10 days, are severe, or you have a high temperature that does not settle.

myth: Grief always follows five stages in a fixed order.
fact: People grieve in many different ways. Feelings such as shock, anger, sadness, guilt and acceptance can come and go, in any order, and there is no right or wrong way or timeline.
explanation: The 'five stages' idea can make people worry they are grieving wrongly. Grief often eases over time, but if it feels overwhelming, stops you functioning for a long time, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, speak to a GP or bereavement service.

sources.label: NHS — Grief after bereavement or loss

myth: Hair analysis, kinesiology or 'bioresonance' machines can diagnose your allergies.
fact: These alternative tests have not been shown to diagnose allergies reliably and are not recommended by health services. Allergies are diagnosed by a doctor using your history together with skin-prick tests, specific blood tests or supervised food challenges.
explanation: Results from unproven tests can wrongly label people as allergic, leading to needless diets, or miss a real and dangerous allergy. If you think you or your child has an allergy, ask a GP, who can refer you to an allergy service if needed.

myth: Hand sanitiser works just as well as soap and water against all germs.
fact: Alcohol-based hand sanitiser is a good option when soap and water are not available, but it does not work as well against some germs, such as norovirus and Clostridioides difficile, and it does not clean visibly dirty or greasy hands well.
explanation: Sanitiser became an everyday habit during the COVID-19 pandemic, and it does kill many germs quickly. Health agencies recommend one with at least 60% alcohol. Washing with soap and water is still preferred when hands are dirty, after using the toilet, and during stomach bugs.

myth: Having a biopsy or surgery makes cancer spread.
fact: The chance that surgery or a biopsy will cause cancer to spread is extremely small. Surgeons follow standard procedures to prevent it, and a biopsy is usually essential for diagnosing cancer and choosing treatment.
explanation: Some people notice that cancer seemed to worsen after an operation and assume the operation caused it. In reality, the cancer may already have spread before it was found. Avoiding a biopsy out of fear can delay treatment that works best when started early.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: Having allergies means your immune system is weak.
fact: An allergy happens when the immune system overreacts to something that is usually harmless, such as pollen, dust mites or a food. It is a misdirected response, not a sign of a weak immune system.
explanation: Allergies are very common and often run in families, along with eczema and asthma. Products that claim to 'boost' the immune system do not cure allergies. Treatments such as antihistamines, nasal sprays and immunotherapy target the allergic response itself.

myth: Having an epidural in labour gives you long-term back pain.
fact: Studies have not found that epidurals cause long-term back pain. Back pain is common after pregnancy whether or not a person had an epidural, because of the strain pregnancy puts on the back.
explanation: The injection site may feel tender for a few days. Epidurals do have possible side effects, such as low blood pressure, itching or, rarely, a severe headache, which the team will explain. Pain relief in labour is a personal choice, and it helps to discuss options with your midwife in advance.

myth: Hay fever gives you a fever.
fact: Despite its name, hay fever does not cause a raised temperature. Its symptoms include sneezing, a runny or blocked nose, itchy red or watery eyes and an itchy throat.
explanation: If you have a high temperature, aching body or feel generally unwell, an infection such as a cold, flu or COVID-19 is more likely. Hay fever symptoms also tend to come with pollen exposure and last for weeks, rather than a few days.

myth: Hay fever only happens in spring.
fact: Different pollens are released at different times: tree pollen mainly in spring, grass pollen in late spring and summer, and weed pollen into early autumn. Some people also have year-round allergic rhinitis from dust mites, pets or mould.
explanation: Knowing which months your symptoms come on can help you work out your triggers. Starting treatments such as antihistamines or steroid nasal sprays before your usual season can help. A pharmacist is a good first point of advice.

myth: HCG drops or injections with a very low-calorie diet melt fat without hunger.
fact: hCG is a pregnancy hormone that is not approved for weight loss. The US Food and Drug Administration warns that over-the-counter hCG diet products are illegal and that there is no substantial evidence they help, and people on these plans lose weight because they eat very little.
explanation: HCG diets typically pair the product with around 500 calories a day, which can cause gallstones, nutrient shortfalls and an irregular heartbeat. Products sold as 'homeopathic' hCG drops contain little or none of the hormone. Safer, effective support for weight loss is available through health services.

sources.label: US FDA — Avoid dangerous hCG diet products

myth: Head lice only affect children with dirty hair or poor hygiene.
fact: Head lice have nothing to do with cleanliness. They spread by direct head-to-head contact, and anyone with hair can get them, whether it is clean or dirty.
explanation: Head lice are common in school-age children because they play closely together. Lice cannot jump or fly, and they do not spread disease. Combing wet hair with a fine-toothed detection comb, or using a lotion or spray from a pharmacy, can treat them; children do not need to be kept off school.

myth: Heart attacks only happen to older people.
fact: Heart attacks are more common with age, but younger adults can have them too, especially if they smoke, have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, obesity or a family history of early heart disease.
explanation: Assuming you are too young can lead people to ignore warning signs and delay calling for help. The build-up of fatty deposits in arteries starts decades before a heart attack. Healthy habits in early adulthood lower lifetime risk.

myth: Heart disease is mainly a men's problem.
fact: Heart and circulatory diseases are a leading cause of death in women as well as men. Women's risk rises after menopause, and women's symptoms are more likely to be missed or put down to other causes.
explanation: Heart disease has long been portrayed as affecting middle-aged men, which has shaped both public perception and research. Women may delay seeking help for symptoms such as breathlessness, fatigue or nausea. Knowing your blood pressure and cholesterol helps whatever your sex.

myth: Herbal remedies don't interact with prescription medicines.
fact: Many herbal products can interact with medicines. For example, St John's wort can make the contraceptive pill, some antidepressants, blood thinners and HIV medicines less effective or cause harmful effects.
explanation: People often don't mention herbal products to their doctor because they think they don't count. Grapefruit juice can also affect how several medicines are processed. Always tell your doctor or pharmacist about any supplements or remedies you take.

myth: Hives are always caused by an allergy.
fact: Hives (urticaria) can be triggered by an allergic reaction, but they can also follow infections, medicines, heat, pressure on the skin, stress or exercise, and often no cause is found. Long-lasting hives are rarely due to allergy.
explanation: Most hives settle within a few days and can be eased with antihistamines from a pharmacy. Hives together with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing, could be anaphylaxis and need emergency help. Hives lasting more than 6 weeks should be seen by a GP.

myth: Homeopathic remedies are effective treatments for illness.
fact: There is no good-quality evidence that homeopathy works for any health condition beyond a placebo effect. Many homeopathic remedies are diluted so much that no molecules of the original substance remain.
explanation: Homeopathy feels gentle and natural, and people often improve as illnesses run their course. The remedies themselves are usually harmless, but the danger comes from using them instead of effective treatment or vaccines. Some products labelled homeopathic have been found to contain measurable active ingredients.

myth: Honey is a safe natural sweetener or cough remedy for babies.
fact: Babies under one year old should not be given honey because it can contain bacteria that cause infant botulism, a serious illness.
explanation: A baby's gut is not mature enough to deal with the bacterial spores. After the first birthday, honey is considered safe and can be used for coughs in children.

myth: How often you eat sugar matters for your teeth, not just how much.
fact: Each time you have sugary food or drinks, bacteria in plaque make acid that attacks the teeth for a while afterwards. Frequent sugary snacks and drinks keep teeth under attack.
explanation: Keeping sugary foods and drinks to mealtimes and cutting down overall both help. Sipping sugary drinks throughout the day is particularly harmful.

myth: HRT gives you breast cancer.
fact: Some types of hormone replacement therapy slightly increase the risk of breast cancer, depending on the type and how long it is taken. For many people the benefits for symptoms outweigh the small risks.
explanation: Oestrogen-only HRT carries little or no increase in breast cancer risk, and vaginal oestrogen is not thought to increase it. Risks and benefits depend on age, health and family history, so the decision is best made with a doctor.

myth: Hydrogen peroxide or strong antiseptic is the best way to clean a cut.
fact: Rinsing a minor cut or graze with clean running water is usually enough to clean it. Hydrogen peroxide and harsh antiseptics can damage healthy tissue and may slow healing.
explanation: The fizzing of peroxide looks like it is killing germs, which makes it seem effective. After rinsing, gently pat the wound dry and cover it with a plaster or dressing. See a doctor for deep, gaping or dirty wounds, animal bites, or signs of infection, and check whether a tetanus booster is needed.

myth: Hydroxychloroquine cures COVID-19.
fact: Large clinical trials, including the UK RECOVERY trial and the WHO Solidarity trial, found that hydroxychloroquine did not reduce deaths in people hospitalised with COVID-19. It is not recommended for treating or preventing COVID-19.
explanation: Hydroxychloroquine was widely promoted early in the pandemic based on lab studies and a small, flawed report. It can cause heart rhythm problems, especially at high doses. It remains a useful medicine for malaria, lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.

myth: If a drink is sugar-free, it can't harm your teeth.
fact: Sugar-free drinks do not cause decay from sugar, but many are acidic and can wear away tooth enamel (dental erosion).
explanation: Fizzy drinks, diet colas, sports drinks and fruit juices can all be acidic. Drinking them with meals, using a straw and choosing water or milk between meals helps protect teeth.

myth: If a home pregnancy test is negative, you're definitely not pregnant.
fact: Home pregnancy tests are accurate when used correctly, but a negative result can be wrong if you test too early, before there is enough pregnancy hormone (hCG) in your urine. Most tests work from the first day of a missed period.
explanation: If you test early and get a negative result but still think you may be pregnant, test again a few days later, ideally with your first urine of the morning. Check the instructions, as tests vary in sensitivity. See a GP if you keep getting negative results but your period has not come.

myth: If an antidepressant hasn't helped after a few days, it isn't working.
fact: Antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect, and it can take 4 to 6 weeks to feel the full benefit. Some side effects may appear before the benefits do.
explanation: It's important not to stop early without talking to your doctor. If a medicine still isn't helping after several weeks, or side effects are hard to manage, the dose or medicine can be changed. If you feel worse or have thoughts of harming yourself, contact a doctor or emergency services straight away.

myth: If it’s natural, it’s automatically safe.
fact: "Natural" does not mean risk-free. Many plants and supplements interact with medications or can be toxic in large doses. Always check with a pharmacist or doctor.
explanation: Many powerful medicines come from plants, which is exactly why natural products can have strong effects. Herbal remedies and supplements can cause side effects, contain contaminants, or interact with prescribed medicines, so tell your doctor or pharmacist what you take.

myth: If no one in my family has had cancer, I won't get it.
fact: Most cancers are not caused by inherited gene changes. Only a minority of cancers, roughly 5 to 10% according to the National Cancer Institute, are strongly linked to inherited mutations; most arise from gene changes that build up during life.
explanation: A strong family history does raise risk for some cancers, which is why it is worth telling your doctor about it. But age, smoking, alcohol, excess weight, sun exposure and some infections are major risk factors for everyone. People without a family history should still take part in screening programmes.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Genetics of cancer
National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: If obesity runs in your family, there is nothing you can do about your weight.
fact: Genes influence appetite, where fat is stored and how easily weight is gained, but for most people they do not decide weight on their own. Eating patterns, activity, sleep and, where appropriate, medical treatment can still make a real difference.
explanation: Families share not only genes but also habits, food and routines, which can be changed. Rare genetic conditions do cause severe obesity from childhood, and these need specialist care. For everyone else, a higher genetic risk means healthy habits matter more, not less.

myth: If someone hears voices, it always means they have schizophrenia.
fact: Hearing voices can be part of psychosis in several conditions, including bipolar disorder, severe depression and drug use, as well as schizophrenia. It can also happen with very little sleep, high fever, grief or brain conditions, and some people hear voices without being unwell.
explanation: Hearing voices that are distressing, or that tell you to do things, should be checked with a GP or mental health service, especially when it is new. Early support for psychosis leads to better outcomes.

myth: If someone is choking, give them water or reach into their mouth to pull the object out.
fact: If someone can cough, encourage them to keep coughing. If they cannot cough, speak or breathe, give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades and then up to 5 abdominal thrusts (chest thrusts for babies), and call emergency services if the blockage does not clear.
explanation: Drinking water can make choking worse, and blind finger sweeps can push the object further down. Only remove an object if you can clearly see it and easily reach it. Anyone who has had abdominal thrusts should be checked by a doctor afterwards. A first aid course is the best way to learn these skills.

sources.label: American Red Cross — Adult & child choking
NHS — How to stop a child from choking

myth: If someone isn't wheezing, they can't be having a serious asthma attack.
fact: Signs of an asthma attack include worsening cough, breathlessness, a tight chest, being unable to finish sentences, and a reliever inhaler that is not helping. In a very severe attack, so little air moves that wheezing can become quiet or disappear.
explanation: Blue or grey lips, confusion, drowsiness or exhaustion are emergency signs. Do not wait for wheezing before following an asthma action plan or calling for help.

myth: If someone swallows poison, make them vomit.
fact: Do not make someone vomit after swallowing a poison or harmful substance unless a medical professional tells you to. Vomiting can cause further damage, especially with corrosive substances, and risks choking. Contact emergency services or a poison centre straight away.
explanation: Syrup of ipecac and salt water were once used to induce vomiting, but these are no longer recommended. Keep the container or packaging to show medical staff what was taken. If the person is unconscious or having trouble breathing, call an ambulance.

myth: If someone swallows something poisonous, give them milk to neutralise it.
fact: Milk does not neutralise poisons. Unless a medical professional advises otherwise, don't give the person anything to eat or drink; instead, get medical help straight away and take the packaging or substance with you.
explanation: Call emergency services if the person is unconscious, having trouble breathing or having a seizure. For other cases, contact a medical helpline or poison centre. Don't try to make them vomit.

myth: If someone who is overheating stops sweating, it means they are cooling down.
fact: Not sweating even though someone feels too hot can be a sign of heatstroke, a medical emergency. Other signs include confusion, a fast heartbeat, fast breathing, a seizure or loss of consciousness.
explanation: Call emergency services, move the person somewhere cool, and cool them with water, wet cloths and fanning while waiting. If they are alert and can swallow, give them water to sip. Heat exhaustion can turn into heatstroke if the person is not cooled down quickly.

myth: If someone with diabetes suddenly becomes shaky, confused or collapses, you should give them insulin.
fact: Sudden shakiness, sweating and confusion in someone with diabetes are often signs of low blood sugar (a 'hypo'), which insulin would make worse. If they are awake and able to swallow, give a sugary drink, sweets or glucose tablets.
explanation: If the person is unconscious, do not give them anything by mouth; put them in the recovery position and call emergency services. Some people carry a glucagon kit that trained family members can use. After a hypo, they should eat a longer-acting carbohydrate snack once they feel better.

myth: If something is stuck in a wound, like a knife or glass, you should pull it out.
fact: Do not remove a large object embedded in a wound, as it may be slowing the bleeding. Apply pressure around the object, not on it, and call emergency services.
explanation: The instinct is to remove the cause of the injury. Pulling the object out can cause heavy bleeding and further damage. Small splinters or surface debris can usually be removed and the wound cleaned with water.

myth: If stroke-like symptoms go away after a few minutes, there's no need to get help.
fact: Symptoms of a stroke that pass quickly may be a transient ischaemic attack (TIA, or 'mini-stroke'). A TIA is a warning sign that a full stroke may follow, so emergency help should still be called, even if the symptoms have gone.
explanation: Use FAST to spot a stroke: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech problems, Time to call emergency services. Prompt assessment and treatment after a TIA greatly lowers the risk of a stroke.

myth: If there's no rash or hives, it can't be anaphylaxis.
fact: Anaphylaxis can happen without any skin rash. Key signs are swelling of the throat or tongue, difficulty breathing or noisy breathing, wheezing, feeling faint or dizzy, and collapse.
explanation: Waiting for a rash before acting can waste vital minutes. If someone has signs of anaphylaxis, use their adrenaline auto-injector if they have one and call emergency services straight away. Anaphylaxis can follow foods, insect stings, medicines or latex.

myth: If you can move it, it isn't broken.
fact: You can sometimes still move a broken bone, especially with small fractures in the hand, wrist, foot or ankle.
explanation: Severe pain, swelling, bruising, deformity or being unable to bear weight are reasons to get an X-ray. Untreated fractures can heal badly.

myth: If you can't sleep, it's best to stay in bed until you drift off.
fact: Sleep experts usually advise getting up if you cannot sleep after a while, doing something calm in dim light, and returning to bed when sleepy.
explanation: Lying awake for long periods can teach the brain to link the bed with frustration. This advice is part of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, which is the recommended first treatment for long-term insomnia.

myth: If you cross your eyes, they'll get stuck that way.
fact: Crossing your eyes on purpose is harmless and they will not stay crossed. The eye muscles relax when you stop.
explanation: A squint that appears on its own, particularly in a child, is different and should be checked by an eye specialist, as early treatment matters.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: If you didn't get knocked out, you can't have concussion.
fact: Most concussions happen without any loss of consciousness. Symptoms can include headache, dizziness, feeling sick, confusion, memory problems and feeling dazed, and they may appear hours after the injury.
explanation: Anyone with a suspected concussion should stop sport or activity and not return the same day. Go to A&E or call emergency services for warning signs such as repeated vomiting, a worsening headache, drowsiness, seizures, weakness or clear fluid from the nose or ears.

myth: If you don't develop PTSD straight after a traumatic event, you won't get it.
fact: Post-traumatic stress disorder can start soon after a traumatic event, but symptoms can also appear weeks, months or even years later.
explanation: Symptoms include flashbacks, nightmares, avoiding reminders, feeling on edge and difficulty sleeping. Many people have distress after trauma that eases over a few weeks; if it doesn't, effective treatments such as trauma-focused therapy are available. Talk to a GP if symptoms are affecting your life.

myth: If you feel tired, you should just take iron tablets.
fact: Iron supplements only help tiredness if you are actually low in iron, which needs a blood test to confirm. Taking iron you don't need can cause constipation and stomach upset, and too much can be toxic.
explanation: Iron deficiency is common, especially in people with heavy periods, pregnancy or restricted diets, so it is a reasonable thing to check. Tiredness has many causes, including poor sleep, thyroid problems, depression and diabetes. Iron overdose is a leading cause of poisoning in young children, so keep tablets out of reach.

myth: If you had prostate cancer, you'd definitely notice symptoms.
fact: Early prostate cancer often causes no symptoms. Urinary symptoms are more commonly caused by a non-cancerous enlarged prostate.
explanation: Because early disease is silent, men with concerns, a family history or higher risk can discuss testing with a doctor, including the pros and cons of a PSA test.

myth: If you have coeliac disease, a little bit of gluten now and then won't hurt.
fact: In coeliac disease, even small amounts of gluten trigger the immune system to damage the lining of the small intestine, whether or not you notice symptoms. The only treatment is a lifelong, strict gluten-free diet.
explanation: Repeated gluten exposure can lead to problems such as anaemia, weakened bones and, rarely, some cancers of the gut. Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition, not a food preference or an intolerance you can 'train' away. A dietitian can help with hidden sources of gluten.

myth: If you have diverticular disease, you must avoid nuts, seeds and popcorn.
fact: Older advice told people with diverticula to avoid nuts, seeds and popcorn, but research has not shown that these foods cause flare-ups. A high-fibre diet is generally recommended to help prevent symptoms.
explanation: During a flare of diverticulitis, a doctor may advise a temporary change in diet. Otherwise, fibre from fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts and seeds helps keep stools soft. Tummy pain with fever or bleeding from the bottom needs medical attention.

myth: If you just relax and stop trying so hard, you'll get pregnant.
fact: Stress can affect sex drive and how often couples have sex, but infertility usually has medical causes, such as problems with ovulation, sperm or the fallopian tubes. Relaxing alone will not fix these.
explanation: Most couples conceive within a year of regular unprotected sex. See a GP if you have not conceived after a year of trying, or sooner if you are 36 or over or know of a possible fertility problem. Being told to 'just relax' can feel dismissive; looking after your wellbeing is worthwhile, but it should not delay getting checked.

myth: If you miss a dose of medicine, take a double dose next time to catch up.
fact: For most medicines you should not take a double dose to make up for a missed one, as this can cause side effects or overdose. The patient leaflet or a pharmacist can tell you what to do for your specific medicine.
explanation: Catching up feels logical, especially with antibiotics. Usually the advice is to take the missed dose when you remember unless it is nearly time for the next one, then carry on as normal. Some medicines, such as the contraceptive pill or insulin, have their own specific rules.

myth: If you pluck a grey hair, two will grow back in its place.
fact: Each hair follicle produces one hair, so plucking cannot make more hairs grow from it.
explanation: Grey hairs often appear in increasing numbers with age, which makes it seem as though plucking caused more. Repeated plucking can damage the follicle, so it is better to trim or colour.

myth: If you relate to ADHD videos on TikTok, you probably have ADHD.
fact: Many ADHD traits, such as getting distracted, losing things or procrastinating, are common in everyone from time to time. ADHD is diagnosed when these difficulties are persistent, started in childhood and cause real problems across different parts of life, which needs a proper assessment.
explanation: Social media has helped many people recognise ADHD and seek help, which can be valuable. But short videos often describe general human experiences, and symptoms like poor concentration can also come from anxiety, depression, poor sleep, thyroid problems or stress. If these difficulties are affecting your life, talking to a GP about an assessment is a better next step than self-diagnosing.

myth: If you stop exercising, your muscle turns into fat.
fact: Muscle and fat are different tissues and one cannot turn into the other. If you stop training, muscles can shrink, and if you eat more than you use, fat can increase.
explanation: Both changes can happen at the same time, which makes it look as if muscle has become fat. Staying somewhat active helps keep muscle as you age.

myth: If you take antibiotics too often, your body becomes resistant to them.
fact: It is bacteria, not your body, that become resistant to antibiotics. Overuse anywhere helps resistant bacteria survive and spread between people, animals and the environment.
explanation: The worry behind the myth is valid: unnecessary antibiotics do cause harm. Resistant bacteria can then infect you or others and be harder to treat. Using antibiotics only when needed, as prescribed, helps keep them working.

myth: If you were once told you're allergic to penicillin, you'll be allergic for life.
fact: Many people labelled as allergic to penicillin are not truly allergic when properly tested, and true penicillin allergy can fade over time. A doctor or allergy specialist can assess whether the label is still accurate.
explanation: Penicillin allergy labels are often added after a childhood rash that may have been caused by the infection itself. Carrying an incorrect label can mean receiving less effective or broader antibiotics. Do not test this yourself; a history of serious reactions needs specialist assessment.

myth: If you're having a heart attack alone, coughing hard repeatedly ('cough CPR') can save you.
fact: 'Cough CPR' is not recommended for the public by heart and resuscitation organisations. If you think you are having a heart attack, call your emergency number immediately.
explanation: This advice has circulated in chain emails for years. Forceful coughing has only been studied in very specific hospital situations under medical supervision. Calling for help, unlocking the door and sitting down while waiting is more useful; emergency call handlers may advise chewing an aspirin if it is safe for you.

myth: If you're lactose intolerant, you must avoid all dairy.
fact: Many people with lactose intolerance can manage small amounts of lactose, especially with meals. Hard cheeses and yoghurt often contain less lactose and may be tolerated, and lactose-free milk is widely available.
explanation: Lactose intolerance is different from a milk allergy, which can be serious and does require avoiding milk. Cutting out dairy completely can reduce calcium intake unless other sources are included. A doctor or dietitian can help confirm the diagnosis and plan your diet.

myth: If you've had the HPV vaccine, you don't need cervical screening.
fact: People who have had the HPV vaccine should still attend cervical screening when invited. The vaccine does not protect against every high-risk HPV type.
explanation: The HPV vaccine greatly lowers the risk of cervical cancer, and screening catches changes the vaccine does not prevent. Together they offer the best protection.

myth: If your blood pressure is normal, you don't need to worry about salt.
fact: Eating too much salt raises blood pressure over time in many people, and most people eat more than WHO's recommended limit of less than 5 grams of salt a day. Cutting down helps prevent high blood pressure, not just treat it.
explanation: Much of the salt we eat is already in bread, processed foods, sauces and ready meals, rather than added at the table. Sea salt and pink salts contain the same sodium as table salt. Checking food labels and cooking from fresh ingredients helps reduce intake.

myth: If your gums bleed, you should stop brushing them.
fact: Bleeding gums are usually a sign of gum inflammation caused by plaque. Gentle, thorough brushing and cleaning between teeth usually helps them recover.
explanation: Avoiding sore areas lets plaque build up and makes things worse. If bleeding continues for more than a couple of weeks, see a dentist. Untreated gum disease can lead to tooth loss.

myth: If your last allergic reaction to a food was mild, the next one will be mild too.
fact: The severity of past reactions does not reliably predict future ones. Someone who has had only mild reactions can still go on to have anaphylaxis, especially with allergies such as peanuts, tree nuts and shellfish.
explanation: Things like the amount eaten, exercise, alcohol, illness and asthma can make a reaction worse. Anyone with a diagnosed food allergy should follow their allergy action plan and carry any prescribed adrenaline auto-injectors.

myth: If your morning sickness is really bad, you must be having a girl.
fact: Some studies have found that very severe sickness in pregnancy (hyperemesis gravidarum) is slightly more common when the baby is a girl, but the difference is small. Many people with severe sickness have boys, so it cannot be used to predict the baby's sex.
explanation: Pregnancy sickness is linked to pregnancy hormones and is also more common in twin pregnancies and in people who had it before. What matters more than the sex is getting help: if you cannot keep food or fluids down, see a GP or midwife, as severe vomiting can be treated.

myth: If your teeth don't hurt, you don't need to see a dentist.
fact: Tooth decay and gum disease often cause no pain until they are advanced. Regular check-ups find problems early, when treatment is simpler.
explanation: How often you need a check-up depends on your oral health; your dentist can advise. Dentists also check for signs of mouth cancer.

myth: In the last three months of pregnancy, going to sleep on your side is safer for the baby than going to sleep on your back.
fact: Research has found that going to sleep on your back after 28 weeks of pregnancy is linked with a higher risk of stillbirth. Health services advise settling down to sleep on your side, either left or right, from 28 weeks, for daytime naps as well as at night.
explanation: Lying on your back late in pregnancy can press on major blood vessels and may reduce blood flow to the baby. If you wake up on your back, there is no need to worry; just turn onto your side. Pillows behind your back can help you stay on your side.

myth: Infertility is usually the woman's problem.
fact: Infertility can be caused by factors in either partner. Problems with sperm are a contributing factor in a substantial share of couples who struggle to conceive.
explanation: Both partners are usually assessed when a couple has difficulty conceiving. Smoking, heavy drinking and obesity can affect fertility in men and women.

myth: Intermittent fasting melts fat much faster than any normal diet, even if you eat the same amount.
fact: Intermittent fasting, such as 16:8 or the 5:2 diet, can help some people lose weight because it often reduces how much they eat overall. In trials that compare it with ordinary daily calorie cutting, weight loss is generally similar.
explanation: Fasting is not a special switch that burns fat regardless of what you eat in the eating window. Some people find time limits make eating less easier; others become very hungry and overeat later. Fasting is not suitable for everyone, including people with a history of eating disorders, people who are pregnant, and people taking some diabetes medicines, who should talk to a doctor first.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — Should you try intermittent fasting for weight loss?

myth: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is all in your head.
fact: IBS is a common, real condition affecting how the gut and brain communicate, causing symptoms such as stomach pain, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation. Stress can trigger or worsen symptoms but is not the only cause.
explanation: Because tests often look normal in IBS, people are sometimes told nothing is wrong. Treatments include diet changes, medicines and psychological therapies, which work on the gut-brain connection rather than meaning symptoms are imagined. Blood in stool, unexplained weight loss or symptoms starting after 50 should be checked by a doctor.

myth: It is better to catch the disease and get natural immunity than to be vaccinated.
fact: Infection can give immunity, but only by risking the disease itself, including serious complications and death. Vaccines produce protection without making you ill with the disease.
explanation: It is true that recovering from some infections, such as measles, gives long-lasting immunity. The problem is the price: measles can cause pneumonia and brain inflammation, and whooping cough can be fatal in babies. Getting infected also means you may pass the illness to vulnerable people before you recover.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: It's fine to take leftover antibiotics or someone else's for a new illness.
fact: Antibiotics should only be taken when prescribed for you and your current infection. A leftover or borrowed antibiotic may be the wrong drug or dose, may not be needed at all, and can cause side effects or allergic reactions.
explanation: Keeping spare antibiotics 'just in case' is common in many households. Taking the wrong antibiotic can delay correct treatment and add to antibiotic resistance. Return unused medicines to a pharmacy.

myth: It's normal for babies to move less towards the end of pregnancy because they run out of room.
fact: Babies should keep moving right up to and during labour. The type of movement may change as the baby grows, but a reduction or change in your baby's usual pattern of movements can be a sign the baby is unwell.
explanation: If you think your baby is moving less, or the pattern has changed, contact your midwife or maternity unit straight away, day or night, rather than waiting until the next day. Do not use home heartbeat monitors to reassure yourself. Most people who get checked are told all is well, but some babies need extra care.

myth: It's safe to doze off with your baby on the sofa or in an armchair as long as you're holding them.
fact: Falling asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair greatly increases the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) and suffocation. If you think you might fall asleep, put the baby down on their back in a cot or Moses basket.
explanation: Babies can slip into gaps between cushions or under an adult's body. The risk is higher if the adult has been drinking, smokes or has taken medicines that cause drowsiness. Night feeds can be exhausting; planning a safe place to put the baby down helps.

myth: It's safe to look at a solar eclipse through ordinary sunglasses.
fact: Ordinary sunglasses do not protect the eyes from a solar eclipse. Looking at the sun can cause permanent damage to the retina.
explanation: Special solar viewing glasses that meet the ISO 12312-2 standard, or indirect methods such as a pinhole projector, are needed. Retina damage can occur without pain.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Ivermectin cures or prevents COVID-19.
fact: Large randomised trials have found that ivermectin does not meaningfully reduce COVID-19 hospitalisation, recovery time or death. It remains an important medicine for certain parasitic infections.
explanation: Early lab results and small, flawed studies led to wide promotion of ivermectin, and some studies were later found to have serious problems. Taking veterinary ivermectin products or high doses has caused poisonings. Proven COVID-19 treatments and vaccines remain the recommended options.

myth: Joints that click or crack are always a sign of damage.
fact: Painless clicking or cracking of joints is common and usually harmless. It is often caused by gas bubbles in joint fluid or tendons moving over bone.
explanation: Noises that come with pain, swelling, locking or the joint giving way are worth getting checked, as they can point to an injury or arthritis.

myth: Lactic acid build-up causes the muscle soreness you feel days after a workout.
fact: Lactate is cleared from muscles within an hour or so of exercise. Delayed soreness is thought to come from small amounts of muscle damage and the repair process.
explanation: Delayed onset muscle soreness usually peaks one to three days after unfamiliar or harder exercise and fades on its own. It lessens as the body adapts.

myth: Lactose intolerance is the same thing as a milk allergy.
fact: Lactose intolerance is a digestive problem where the body does not make enough of the enzyme needed to digest milk sugar, causing wind, bloating and diarrhoea. A milk allergy is a reaction of the immune system to milk proteins and can cause rashes, swelling and, rarely, life-threatening anaphylaxis.
explanation: The difference matters because many people with lactose intolerance can manage small amounts of dairy or lactose-free products, while people with a milk allergy usually need to avoid milk protein entirely. Milk allergy is more common in babies and young children. A doctor can help work out which one is responsible for symptoms.

myth: Lifestyle changes can stop prediabetes from turning into type 2 diabetes.
fact: In people with prediabetes, losing a modest amount of weight and being more active can greatly lower the chance of developing type 2 diabetes. In the US Diabetes Prevention Program trial, a lifestyle programme cut the risk by 58% over about three years.
explanation: Some people see prediabetes as inevitable diabetes. Losing around 5 to 7% of body weight and doing about 150 minutes of activity a week were the goals in the major trial. Structured prevention programmes are available in several countries.

myth: Lifting weights or doing strength training will stunt a child's growth.
fact: There is no good evidence that properly supervised strength training stunts growth. The WHO recommends that children and teenagers include muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least 3 days a week.
explanation: Physical activity in childhood supports healthy bones and muscles. Injuries in young people lifting weights are mostly linked to poor technique, too-heavy loads or lack of supervision. Bodyweight exercises, climbing and play count as strengthening activity for younger children.

myth: Lifting weights will make women bulky.
fact: Strength training builds strength and bone health in women, but large increases in muscle size are difficult to achieve and usually need specific, intensive training and diet.
explanation: Women typically have lower testosterone levels than men, which limits muscle growth. Guidelines recommend muscle-strengthening activities for all adults at least two days a week.

myth: Liver detox supplements and teas cleanse your liver after drinking or unhealthy eating.
fact: A healthy liver clears waste and alcohol by itself, and no supplement has been shown to 'detox' it. Some herbal and dietary supplements can actually damage the liver.
explanation: The best ways to protect your liver are to drink less alcohol, keep to a healthy weight and get vaccinated against hepatitis B if advised. Liver disease often causes no symptoms until it is advanced, so people with heavy drinking or other risk factors may need blood tests rather than detox products.

sources.label: NCCIH — "Detoxes" and "cleanses": what you need to know

myth: Losing even a small amount of weight can improve your health.
fact: For people living with overweight or obesity, losing around 5 to 10% of body weight can improve blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar and lower the risk of type 2 diabetes.
explanation: Many people feel discouraged because they are far from their 'ideal' weight. Health benefits start well before that point. Being more active and eating better can also improve health independently of weight change.

myth: Losing weight slowly and steadily is more likely to last than losing it fast.
fact: Health services generally advise aiming to lose about 0.5 to 1 kg (1 to 2 lb) a week through lasting changes to eating and activity. Habits you can keep up are the key to keeping weight off.
explanation: Very rapid weight loss from extreme diets tends to include water and muscle, can cause gallstones, and is often regained. That said, some medically supervised low-calorie programmes produce faster early loss and can work well for some people with support. The overall message is to choose a plan you can maintain.

myth: Low-fat or 'light' products are always healthier and help you lose weight.
fact: Some low-fat products have extra sugar or other ingredients added to improve taste, so they may not be lower in calories. Reading nutrition labels gives a better picture than the 'low-fat' claim alone.
explanation: Choosing lower-fat versions of some foods, like milk or cooking methods, can reduce saturated fat and calories. But a 'light' label can encourage eating larger amounts. Unsaturated fats from foods like nuts, olive oil and oily fish are part of a healthy diet.

myth: Lying with your legs up in the air after sex helps you get pregnant.
fact: There is no good evidence that lying with your legs raised, or any particular sex position, makes pregnancy more likely. Sperm reach the cervix within minutes of ejaculation, whatever position you are in.
explanation: What makes the biggest difference is having regular sex, every two to three days, throughout the cycle. Some semen leaking out afterwards is normal and does not reduce your chances. If you enjoy lying down for a while, it does no harm.

myth: Lymphatic drainage massage flushes out toxins, de-bloats you and helps you lose weight.
fact: Manual lymphatic drainage is a specialised massage used, with compression and exercise, to help manage lymphoedema, a condition where fluid builds up because the lymphatic system is damaged. There is no good evidence that it removes 'toxins' or reduces body fat in healthy people.
explanation: Any slimmer look after a session is temporary fluid movement. Massage can feel relaxing, which is a perfectly good reason to have one, but it is not a weight-loss treatment. Swelling in one limb or that does not go away should be checked by a doctor rather than treated with home massage.

sources.label: NCCIH — Massage therapy: what you need to know

myth: Many people need a vitamin D supplement in winter.
fact: In countries with little winter sunshine, such as the UK, health authorities advise considering a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter, because the body cannot make enough from sunlight then. Some groups are advised to take it all year.
explanation: Advice varies by country, skin colour, age and lifestyle, so this does not apply to everyone everywhere. People with darker skin, those who cover their skin or rarely go outdoors, and some older adults are at higher risk of low vitamin D. Taking very high doses for long periods can be harmful.

sources.label: NIH ODS — Vitamin D fact sheet

myth: Measles is a mild childhood illness that everyone used to get.
fact: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases and can cause pneumonia, brain inflammation (encephalitis), blindness and death. WHO estimates that it still kills more than 100,000 people a year worldwide, mostly young children.
explanation: Older generations often remember measles as a normal part of childhood, and many children did recover. But the deaths and disabilities it caused were also common before vaccination. Measles can also weaken the immune system for months or years afterwards.

myth: Melatonin is a natural, harmless sleeping pill everyone can take.
fact: Melatonin can help with some sleep problems, such as jet lag or certain body clock disorders, but its effect on general insomnia is modest. It can cause side effects and interact with medicines.
explanation: In some countries melatonin is prescription-only; in others it is sold as a supplement whose actual content can differ from the label. Children and pregnant people should only use it on medical advice.

myth: Men can't get breast cancer.
fact: Men have breast tissue and can get breast cancer, although it is much rarer than in women.
explanation: It usually affects older men. A lump, nipple changes or discharge should be checked by a doctor rather than ignored.

myth: Men don't really get depression; real men just tough it out.
fact: Men do get depression, but they are less likely to be diagnosed or to seek help. In many countries men die by suicide at higher rates than women.
explanation: In men, depression may show as anger, irritability, risk-taking, heavy drinking or overworking. Asking for help is a strength. Talking to a GP, doctor or helpline is a good first step, and anyone in crisis should contact emergency services or a crisis line.

myth: Men go through a menopause just like women.
fact: Testosterone falls gradually in men, by a small amount each year from around 30 to 40, rather than dropping suddenly as oestrogen does at menopause. True testosterone deficiency is uncommon.
explanation: Symptoms often blamed on a 'male menopause', such as low mood, tiredness or low sex drive, are frequently linked to stress, lifestyle, depression or other health problems. A doctor can check what is going on.

myth: Menopause is just hot flushes and periods stopping.
fact: Menopause can bring a wide range of symptoms, including sleep problems, low mood, anxiety, brain fog, joint aches, vaginal dryness and reduced sex drive, as well as hot flushes.
explanation: Lower oestrogen after menopause also increases the risk of osteoporosis. Symptoms vary a lot between people; treatments including hormone replacement therapy and non-hormonal options can help.

myth: Menopause only happens in your fifties.
fact: The average age of menopause is around 51, but it can happen earlier. Menopause before 45 is called early menopause and before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency.
explanation: Perimenopause symptoms can start several years before periods stop. Early menopause can also follow surgery or cancer treatment. Anyone with symptoms at a younger age should see a doctor, as treatment may protect bones and heart.

myth: Microwaving destroys all the nutrients in food.
fact: All cooking methods change nutrients to some degree. Microwaving often keeps nutrients as well as or better than boiling, because it uses shorter cooking times and less water.
explanation: Some vitamins, such as vitamin C and some B vitamins, are sensitive to heat and leak into cooking water. Because microwaving is quick and uses little water, vegetables can keep more of these vitamins. Steaming is another good option.

myth: Microwaving food makes it radioactive or causes cancer.
fact: Microwave ovens heat food using non-ionising radiation that makes water molecules vibrate. This does not make food radioactive or change it in a way that causes cancer, and ovens are built to keep microwaves inside.
explanation: The word 'radiation' makes many people think of nuclear radiation, which is a different, high-energy type. A real safety point is to use microwave-safe containers, because some plastics not designed for heating can warp or leach chemicals. Damaged ovens with doors that do not close properly should be repaired or replaced.

myth: Miracle Mineral Solution (MMS, chlorine dioxide) cures autism, COVID-19 and other diseases.
fact: MMS becomes chlorine dioxide, a type of industrial bleach, when mixed as instructed. It has no proven health benefits and can cause severe vomiting, diarrhoea, dangerously low blood pressure and life-threatening reactions.
explanation: MMS has been promoted online and in private groups as a cure for autism, cancer, HIV and COVID-19. US regulators have warned consumers not to buy or drink it, and sellers have been prosecuted. If someone has swallowed it and is unwell, contact a poison centre or emergency services.

myth: Miscarriage is rare and usually happens because the mother did something wrong.
fact: Miscarriage is common: about 1 in 8 known pregnancies ends in miscarriage, and many more happen before a person knows they are pregnant. Most early miscarriages are caused by chromosome problems in the baby and are not caused by anything the mother did.
explanation: Normal activities such as work, exercise, sex or a fall or shock are not usually the cause. Having one miscarriage does not mean you will not have a successful pregnancy next time. If you have had three or more in a row, doctors may offer tests to look for a cause.

myth: Mobile phones and 5G cause brain cancer.
fact: Large studies have not found consistent evidence that mobile phone use causes brain tumours or other cancers. Mobile phones and 5G networks use non-ionising radio waves, which do not damage DNA the way X-rays or UV light can.
explanation: In 2011 the International Agency for Research on Cancer classed radiofrequency fields as 'possibly carcinogenic', a category meaning evidence is limited and inconclusive, which is often misreported. Brain cancer rates have not risen in line with the huge growth in phone use. Using a headset or speaker reduces exposure for anyone who wants to be cautious.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Cell phones and cancer risk
National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: Morning sickness only happens in the morning.
fact: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy can happen at any time of day or night.
explanation: It usually eases by around 16 to 20 weeks. Severe vomiting where you cannot keep fluids down may be hyperemesis gravidarum, which needs prompt medical care.

myth: mRNA COVID-19 vaccines change your DNA.
fact: mRNA vaccines never enter the cell nucleus, where DNA is kept, and cannot alter your genes. The mRNA gives cells temporary instructions to make a harmless protein, and it is broken down by the body within days.
explanation: The word 'genetic' in descriptions of mRNA technology led many people to assume it edits genes. Human cells read mRNA all the time as a normal part of making proteins. The vaccine mRNA is fragile, which is why some of these vaccines had to be kept very cold.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: MSG (monosodium glutamate) is dangerous and causes 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'.
fact: MSG is considered safe to eat by food safety agencies, including the US FDA. Studies have not consistently shown that MSG causes headaches or other symptoms in normal amounts eaten with food.
explanation: The term 'Chinese restaurant syndrome' came from a 1968 letter and spread with little evidence, and it has been criticised as reflecting bias. Glutamate occurs naturally in foods such as tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms. A small number of people may report short-lived mild symptoms after large amounts of MSG without food.

sources.label: FDA — Questions and answers on monosodium glutamate (MSG)

myth: Napping during the day always ruins your night's sleep.
fact: Short naps of around 20 to 30 minutes early in the afternoon can improve alertness without harming night sleep for most people.
explanation: Long or late naps can make it harder to fall asleep at night, so people with insomnia are often advised to avoid them. A strong need to nap every day can also be a sign of poor night sleep worth looking into.

myth: Needing your blue reliever inhaler several times a week is normal if you have asthma.
fact: When asthma is well controlled, most people rarely need their reliever inhaler. Needing it 3 or more times a week is a sign that asthma is not well controlled and should be reviewed by a doctor or asthma nurse.
explanation: Often the answer is a regular preventer inhaler, a different treatment or a better inhaler technique. Relying on a reliever alone leaves the underlying inflammation untreated and raises the risk of a serious attack.

myth: No pain, no gain: exercise only works if it hurts.
fact: Exercise does not need to be painful to be beneficial. Moderate activity that makes you breathe harder but still lets you talk brings major health benefits.
explanation: Some muscle soreness a day or two after new or harder exercise is normal. Sharp pain, joint pain or chest pain during exercise is a signal to stop and get it checked.

myth: Not getting enough sleep can make it harder to manage your weight.
fact: Regularly sleeping too little is linked to a higher risk of weight gain and obesity. Short sleep can affect hormones that control hunger and fullness and tends to increase snacking and cravings for high-calorie food.
explanation: Most of the evidence comes from observational studies and short experiments, so sleep is one factor among many rather than the main cause of weight gain. Still, aiming for enough regular sleep is a useful part of any plan to manage weight. Ongoing sleep problems, such as loud snoring with pauses in breathing, are worth discussing with a doctor.

sources.label: NHLBI — Sleep deprivation and deficiency: health effects

myth: Numbing gels from the pharmacy are the safest go-to for a teething baby.
fact: Gels containing benzocaine or lidocaine offer little benefit for teething and have been linked to serious side effects in young children, including a rare blood disorder (methaemoglobinaemia) with benzocaine. The US FDA advises against using them for teething.
explanation: Products sold for teething vary by country, so always check the ingredients and age guidance and ask a pharmacist. Homeopathic teething tablets are also not recommended. A chilled teething ring, gum massage and, if needed, infant paracetamol or ibuprofen at the right dose are the usual advice.

sources.label: FDA — Safely soothing teething pain in infants and children

myth: OCD just means being very neat and tidy.
fact: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is a mental health condition with unwanted, distressing thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours (compulsions) that take up a lot of time and interfere with life.
explanation: Liking things orderly is a personality trait, not OCD. Obsessions in OCD can be about contamination, harm, doubt or many other themes, and treatments such as CBT with exposure and response prevention help.
