myth: Okra water, bitter gourd (karela) juice or fenugreek can cure diabetes.
fact: There is no good evidence that okra water, bitter melon, fenugreek or similar home remedies cure diabetes. Some may have small effects on blood sugar, but they are not a substitute for proven treatment.
explanation: These remedies are widely shared on WhatsApp and in family traditions. Combining them with diabetes medicines can sometimes lower blood sugar too much. Eating these vegetables as part of a balanced diet is fine, but talk to your diabetes team before relying on them.

myth: Older people can't learn new things because the brain stops changing after childhood.
fact: The brain stays able to change and form new connections throughout life. Older adults can learn new skills, languages and habits.
explanation: Learning may take a little longer with age, but practice, motivation and staying active all help. Learning new things is also thought to support brain health.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Older people need less sleep.
fact: Older adults need about the same amount of sleep as younger adults, around seven to nine hours. Sleep tends to become lighter and more broken with age, which can make it harder to get.
explanation: Changes in body clock, health conditions, medicines and needing the toilet at night can reduce sleep in later life. Ongoing poor sleep is not something to accept as normal and can often be improved.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Once you have a mental illness you never get better.
fact: Many people recover fully or manage their symptoms well with treatment and support. Recovery is common, though it can take time and may involve setbacks.
explanation: Some conditions are long-term, but treatment, therapy, medication and social support can let people live full lives. Getting help early generally improves outcomes. If you are struggling, talking to a GP, a doctor or a mental health helpline is a good first step.

myth: Once you've had a caesarean, all your future babies have to be born by caesarean.
fact: Many people who have had a caesarean can safely have a vaginal birth next time, known as VBAC (vaginal birth after caesarean). Most of those who plan a VBAC give birth vaginally.
explanation: Whether VBAC is a good option depends on the reason for the previous caesarean, the type of cut in the womb, how many caesareans you have had and your current pregnancy. There is a small risk of the scar opening during labour, so labour is monitored in hospital. Your midwife or obstetrician can help you weigh up the choices.

sources.label: ACOG — Vaginal birth after cesarean delivery

myth: Once you've lost weight on injections like Wegovy or Ozempic, you can stop them and the weight will stay off.
fact: Medicines such as semaglutide can help people with obesity lose a meaningful amount of weight when used alongside changes to diet and activity. In studies, many people regained much of the lost weight within a year of stopping the medicine.
explanation: These medicines work by reducing appetite, and appetite tends to return when they are stopped. They can also cause side effects such as nausea, vomiting and constipation, and should only be used under medical supervision, not bought from unregulated online sellers. Building eating and activity habits during treatment gives the best chance of keeping weight off.

sources.label: NIDDK — Prescription medications to treat overweight & obesity

myth: Once your blood pressure is normal, you can stop taking your tablets.
fact: Blood pressure is often normal because the medicine is working. Stopping without medical advice usually lets it rise again, increasing the risk of stroke and heart attack.
explanation: People often feel well and see a normal reading, so assume they are cured. Some people can reduce or stop medication after lasting lifestyle changes, but this should be done with a doctor and with monitoring. Never stop suddenly without advice, as some medicines need to be reduced gradually.

sources.label: American Heart Association — High blood pressure

myth: Only elderly people get dementia.
fact: Dementia mostly affects older people, but it can begin before 65. This is called young-onset dementia.
explanation: Young-onset dementia can be missed because symptoms are blamed on stress, depression or menopause. Anyone with ongoing changes in memory, behaviour or thinking should see a doctor.

myth: Only heavy drinkers get fatty liver disease.
fact: Fatty liver disease that is not caused by alcohol is very common and is mainly linked to being overweight, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol. It often causes no symptoms in its early stages.
explanation: This condition is now often called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), previously non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Early stages can improve with weight loss, regular activity and a healthy diet. Without changes, it can progress to scarring of the liver in some people.

myth: Only old people get arthritis.
fact: Arthritis can affect people of any age, including children. Rheumatoid arthritis often starts between 30 and 50, and juvenile arthritis affects children.
explanation: Osteoarthritis does become more common with age. Joint pain, swelling or stiffness that lasts should be checked at any age, because early treatment of inflammatory arthritis can prevent damage.

myth: Only overweight people get type 2 diabetes.
fact: Excess weight is a major risk factor, but people of a healthy weight can also get type 2 diabetes. Age, family history, ethnicity and where fat is stored on the body also affect risk.
explanation: People of South Asian, Black African and Black Caribbean backgrounds, for example, can develop type 2 diabetes at a lower body weight. Fat stored around the waist and organs raises risk even when overall weight looks normal. Anyone with symptoms like excess thirst, frequent urination or unexplained tiredness should get checked.

myth: Only soldiers get PTSD.
fact: Post-traumatic stress disorder can follow any traumatic event, such as an assault, accident, disaster, sudden loss or difficult childbirth.
explanation: PTSD was first widely studied in veterans, which is why the link persists. Not everyone exposed to trauma develops PTSD, and effective therapies exist.

myth: Only trained medical staff should use a defibrillator, because you could shock someone who doesn't need it.
fact: Public-access defibrillators (AEDs) are designed for anyone to use. They give spoken instructions and analyse the heart rhythm, delivering a shock only if it is needed.
explanation: If someone collapses and is not breathing normally, call emergency services, start CPR and ask someone to fetch the nearest AED. Using an AED quickly, alongside CPR, greatly improves the chance of survival from cardiac arrest.

sources.label: American Red Cross — Using an AED

myth: Only very old men need to think about prostate cancer.
fact: Prostate cancer is most common in men over 50 and risk rises with age, but it can occur earlier, particularly in men with a family history or of Black ethnicity.
explanation: Men in higher-risk groups are often advised to talk to a doctor about testing from a younger age. Many prostate cancers grow slowly, so decisions about testing and treatment are individual.

myth: Only women get osteoporosis.
fact: Osteoporosis is more common in women, especially after menopause, but men get it too, and men with hip fractures have a high risk of complications.
explanation: Risk factors in men include older age, low testosterone, smoking, heavy drinking, long-term steroid use and some medical conditions. Many men are never tested.

myth: Only young women get eating disorders.
fact: Eating disorders affect people of all genders, ages, body sizes and backgrounds. Men and older adults are often under-diagnosed.
explanation: The stereotype can stop people from recognising a problem or seeking help. A person does not have to look underweight to have a serious eating disorder. Early treatment improves recovery.

myth: Organic food is much more nutritious than non-organic food.
fact: Studies have not found consistent, meaningful differences in vitamins and minerals between organic and conventionally grown foods. Organic produce tends to have lower pesticide residues, but residues on conventional food are generally within safety limits.
explanation: People choose organic for many reasons, including environmental and animal welfare concerns, which are valid personal choices. From a nutrition point of view, eating plenty of fruit and vegetables matters more than whether they are organic. Washing produce under running water is sensible either way.

myth: Over-the-counter testosterone booster supplements reliably raise testosterone and build muscle.
fact: There is little good evidence that most testosterone booster supplements meaningfully raise testosterone or build muscle in healthy men.
explanation: Supplements are not tested like medicines, and some have been found to contain undeclared ingredients. Men worried about low testosterone should see a doctor, who can test levels and look for underlying causes.

myth: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is so safe you can't take too much.
fact: Paracetamol is safe at recommended doses, but taking too much, even a little over the limit for several days, can cause serious liver damage. Many cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol, making accidental overdose easy.
explanation: Because it is sold everywhere, many people assume paracetamol is harmless at any dose. Early overdose may cause no symptoms, so anyone who has taken too much should get urgent medical advice even if they feel well. Check labels to avoid taking two products that both contain it.

myth: Passing wind many times a day means something is wrong with your digestion.
fact: Passing gas is a normal part of digestion, and most people pass wind several times or more each day. Gas comes from swallowed air and from gut bacteria breaking down food, especially fibre-rich foods such as beans and vegetables.
explanation: More wind after eating healthy, high-fibre food is common and usually harmless. It is worth seeing a doctor if gas comes with tummy pain, ongoing diarrhoea or constipation, weight loss or blood in your poo. Eating more slowly and adjusting trigger foods can help if wind is bothersome.

sources.label: NIDDK — Gas in the digestive tract

myth: Peeing on a jellyfish sting relieves the pain.
fact: Urine does not help jellyfish stings and may make the stinging cells release more venom. Rinse the area with seawater rather than fresh water, remove any tentacles carefully, and soak the area in hot (not scalding) water if possible.
explanation: This myth was popularised by a television sitcom and spread widely. Some advice, such as using vinegar, depends on the type of jellyfish, so follow local lifeguard guidance. Severe pain, breathing difficulty or stings to a large area need urgent medical help.

sources.label: NHS — Jellyfish and other sea creature stings

myth: Peeing, washing or douching straight after sex stops you getting pregnant.
fact: None of these prevent pregnancy. Sperm can reach the cervix within minutes, urine comes out of a different opening (the urethra), and douching does not remove sperm that have already entered the womb.
explanation: If you have had sex without contraception, or contraception failed, emergency contraception can prevent pregnancy if used soon enough. The copper IUD is the most effective option and works up to 5 days after sex. Peeing after sex may help reduce urine infections, but it is not contraception.

myth: People are either left-brained (logical) or right-brained (creative).
fact: Although some functions are more concentrated on one side of the brain, people do not have a dominant hemisphere that defines their personality or thinking style.
explanation: Large brain-imaging studies have found no evidence for left-brained or right-brained people. Both sides work together for most tasks, including logic and creativity.

myth: People who are overweight have a slow metabolism.
fact: People with a larger body usually burn more energy at rest, not less, because there is more body tissue to maintain. Differences in metabolism between people of similar size are generally small.
explanation: Metabolism is often blamed for weight gain because it feels outside our control. Some medical conditions, such as an underactive thyroid, and some medicines can affect weight. Appetite, food environment, sleep, stress and activity levels all play a larger role for most people.

myth: People who had a COVID-19 vaccine 'shed' it and make others sick.
fact: None of the widely used COVID-19 vaccines contain live virus, so there is nothing that can be shed and passed to other people. The spike protein made after vaccination stays in the body and is cleared over time.
explanation: The idea of 'shedding' comes from some live vaccines, such as oral polio vaccine, where weakened virus can be passed on in rare cases. That does not apply to mRNA or protein-based vaccines. Claims that vaccinated people affect others' periods or health have not been supported by evidence.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: People who self-harm are just seeking attention.
fact: Self-harm is usually a way of coping with overwhelming emotions, distress or trauma, and many people who self-harm hide it. It is a sign that someone needs support, not something to dismiss.
explanation: Responding calmly and without judgement makes it easier for someone to open up. If you are self-harming, or worried about someone who is, please talk to a GP, a trusted person or a mental health helpline. If someone is seriously injured or at immediate risk, call emergency services.

myth: People who talk about suicide won't actually do it; they just want attention.
fact: Many people who die by suicide have spoken about it beforehand. Talk of suicide should always be taken seriously.
explanation: Talking about wanting to die or being a burden are recognised warning signs. Responding with care, listening and helping the person reach support can save a life. If there is immediate danger, contact emergency services or a crisis line.

myth: People with asthma shouldn't exercise.
fact: Regular exercise is good for people with asthma and can improve fitness and lung health. With asthma well controlled and the right preparation, most people with asthma can exercise fully, and many elite athletes have asthma.
explanation: Exercise can trigger symptoms in some people, which leads them to avoid it. A doctor or asthma nurse can help adjust treatment, which may include using a reliever inhaler before exercise. Warming up and avoiding very cold, dry air can also help.

myth: People with dark skin don't need sun protection.
fact: Darker skin has more natural protection against burning, but it can still be damaged by UV and people with dark skin can get skin cancer.
explanation: Skin cancer in people with darker skin is often found later, when it is harder to treat, and can appear in less sun-exposed places such as the palms, soles or under nails. Sun protection is still advised when UV is high.

myth: People with diabetes can never eat any sugar or sweets.
fact: People with diabetes can include small amounts of sugar as part of a balanced diet, planned around their meals, activity and medication. The overall pattern of eating matters more than avoiding sugar completely.
explanation: Diabetes eating advice used to be very strict, and many people still believe sugar is completely banned. Carbohydrates in general, including bread, rice and pasta, affect blood sugar, not just sweets. People who use insulin or some tablets may actually need fast-acting sugar to treat a low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia).

sources.label: NIDDK — Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity

myth: People with diabetes need to buy special 'diabetic' foods.
fact: There is no need for special 'diabetic' foods. People with diabetes are advised to eat the same healthy, balanced diet recommended for everyone.
explanation: Products labelled 'diabetic' or 'suitable for diabetics' are often expensive and can still be high in fat and calories. Some contain sugar alcohols that can cause bloating and diarrhoea. Reading normal food labels is usually more helpful.

sources.label: NIDDK — Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity

myth: People with diabetes shouldn't eat fruit because it has sugar.
fact: Whole fruit contains fibre, vitamins and minerals and can be part of a healthy diet for people with diabetes. Portion size and spreading fruit through the day matter more than avoiding it.
explanation: The natural sugar in fruit leads many people to cut it out. Whole fruit is a better choice than fruit juice or dried fruit, which raise blood sugar more quickly. A dietitian or diabetes team can help plan portions.

sources.label: NIDDK — Diabetes diet, eating and physical activity

myth: People with mental illness are usually violent and dangerous.
fact: Most people with mental health conditions are not violent. They are more likely to be victims of violence than to commit it.
explanation: Media stories often link violence with mental illness, which feeds stigma. Factors such as substance misuse and past violence are stronger predictors of violence than a mental health diagnosis alone.

myth: Peppermint oil capsules can ease the symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome.
fact: Studies suggest enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules can help relieve tummy pain and bloating in some people with IBS. It is one of the options health services suggest trying.
explanation: Peppermint oil can cause heartburn in some people, which is why coated capsules are used. It does not work for everyone, and IBS symptoms such as unexplained weight loss or bleeding should be checked by a doctor before assuming it is IBS. Other helpful steps include adjusting fibre, regular meals and managing stress.

myth: Picking up a crying baby too often will spoil them.
fact: Young babies cannot be spoiled by being comforted. Responding to their needs helps them feel secure.
explanation: Crying is how babies communicate hunger, discomfort or the need for closeness. If crying is constant or you feel overwhelmed, it is fine to put the baby down safely and take a short break, and to seek help from a health visitor or doctor.

myth: Popping pimples helps them heal faster.
fact: Squeezing spots can push bacteria deeper, increase inflammation and lead to scarring. It is better to leave them alone.
explanation: Popping can seem to give a quick fix, but it often makes the spot last longer. Persistent or painful acne can be treated with products from a pharmacist or prescriptions from a doctor.

myth: Postnatal depression is just the 'baby blues' and goes away on its own.
fact: The baby blues, with tearfulness and low mood, are common in the first two weeks after birth and usually pass. Postnatal depression lasts longer, can start any time in the first year, and is a real illness that usually needs support and treatment.
explanation: Signs include persistent sadness, loss of interest, difficulty bonding with the baby, and frightening thoughts. Partners can be affected too. Having postnatal depression does not mean someone is a bad parent. Speak to a midwife, health visitor or GP; if anyone has thoughts of harming themselves or the baby, get urgent help.

myth: Pregnant women should avoid all vaccines because they could harm the baby.
fact: Some vaccines are specifically recommended in pregnancy, including whooping cough (pertussis), flu and, in many countries, RSV and COVID-19 vaccines. They protect the mother and pass antibodies to the baby, protecting it in the first weeks of life before it can be vaccinated.
explanation: These vaccines have been given to very large numbers of pregnant people and are closely monitored for safety. Live vaccines, such as MMR, are usually avoided in pregnancy as a precaution, which is why it helps to check your vaccinations before trying to conceive. Your midwife or GP can tell you which vaccines are due and when.

myth: Pricking a stroke victim's fingertips or earlobes with a needle to let out blood can save them.
fact: There is no evidence that bloodletting from the fingers or ears helps someone having a stroke. The only effective first aid is to call emergency services immediately so the person can get hospital treatment quickly.
explanation: This advice has circulated for years in chain messages. Strokes caused by a clot can sometimes be treated with clot-busting medicines or a procedure to remove the clot, but only within hours, so every minute matters. Don't give the person anything to eat or drink while waiting for help.

myth: Probiotic supplements improve everyone's health.
fact: Some specific probiotic strains may help with certain problems, such as reducing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. But benefits depend on the strain and the condition, and there is little evidence that healthy people gain general health benefits from taking them.
explanation: Interest in the gut microbiome has led to many bold marketing claims. Probiotics are generally safe for healthy people but have caused serious infections in rare cases in very ill or immunocompromised patients, including premature babies. Foods like yoghurt and kefir can be part of a varied diet.

myth: Put a hot water bottle or heat pad on a fresh sprain to help it heal.
fact: For the first few days after a sprain or strain, health services advise rest, ice (wrapped in a towel), compression and raising the injured area. Heat, along with alcohol, running and massage, should be avoided early on because it can increase swelling.
explanation: After the first few days, gentle movement helps recovery. See a doctor if you can't put weight on the injury, if it looks deformed, or if the pain and swelling do not start to improve.

myth: Put a raw steak on a black eye.
fact: A black eye is best treated with a cold compress, such as an ice pack or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel, held gently on the area for a few minutes at a time. Raw meat is not recommended, as it can carry bacteria that may cause infection.
explanation: The cold reduces swelling, and any cold object would do the same job as the steak once did. Get urgent help if there are vision changes, blood in the eye, severe pain, or a head injury with vomiting or drowsiness.

myth: Put butter, oil or toothpaste on a burn.
fact: Butter, oil, toothpaste and similar home remedies should not be put on burns. They can trap heat, delay cooling and increase the risk of infection. The recommended first step is to cool the burn under cool or lukewarm running water.
explanation: These remedies are passed down in families and may feel soothing at first. After cooling, a burn can be loosely covered with cling film or a clean plastic bag. Get medical help for large or deep burns, burns on the face, hands, feet or genitals, and burns in children.

myth: Put something in a person's mouth during a seizure so they don't swallow their tongue.
fact: It is impossible to swallow your tongue. Never put anything in the mouth of someone having a seizure, as it can break teeth, injure the jaw or cause choking. Protect their head, move hazards away and time the seizure.
explanation: Seizures can be frightening to watch, and people want to do something to help. Once the jerking stops, put the person on their side in the recovery position. Call an ambulance if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, it is their first seizure, or they are injured or do not wake up.

myth: Putting a jaundiced newborn in direct sunlight by a window will cure the jaundice.
fact: Newborn jaundice that needs treatment is treated with phototherapy: special blue lights used in a controlled setting with the baby's temperature and eyes protected. Direct sunlight is not a safe or reliable treatment and can cause sunburn or overheating.
explanation: Mild jaundice is common in the first week and often clears on its own with good feeding. Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life, a very yellow or drowsy baby, pale poo or jaundice lasting more than 2 weeks needs to be checked by a midwife or doctor. A simple blood test shows whether treatment is needed.

myth: Putting a newborn to sleep in their own room from the start is safest and teaches independence.
fact: Health services advise that babies sleep in a cot or Moses basket in the same room as a parent or carer for at least the first 6 months, for day and night sleeps. This lowers the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
explanation: Room-sharing is different from bed-sharing: the baby sleeps on their own separate surface next to you. Sleeping in a separate room in the early months has no proven benefit for independence. Talk to your health visitor if you have questions about safe sleep arrangements.

myth: Putting an aspirin directly on a sore tooth helps toothache.
fact: Placing aspirin against the gum or tooth does not work better than swallowing it and can cause a painful chemical burn to the gum.
explanation: Painkillers work when taken by mouth as directed. Toothache often means decay or infection, so see a dentist. Facial swelling with fever or trouble swallowing needs urgent care.

myth: Putting an unconscious person who is breathing on their side (the recovery position) helps keep their airway clear.
fact: Placing an unresponsive person who is breathing normally on their side helps keep the airway open and lets vomit or fluid drain out of the mouth rather than being breathed in.
explanation: Call emergency services and keep checking their breathing. If they stop breathing normally, roll them onto their back and start CPR. If you suspect a spinal injury, try to keep the head and neck in line when moving them.

sources.label: American Red Cross — Unresponsive and breathing person

myth: Putting coffee powder, turmeric or ash on a cut stops the bleeding and prevents infection.
fact: The recommended way to stop bleeding is to press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or dressing and, if possible, raise it. Powders and household substances are not sterile and can make infection more likely and wound cleaning harder.
explanation: Once bleeding stops, rinse the cut under clean running water and cover it with a plaster or dressing. Seek medical help if bleeding is heavy or won't stop, the cut is deep or gaping, or there is something stuck in it.

myth: Putting ice on a burn is the best way to cool it down.
fact: Ice, iced water and very cold packs can damage the skin further. Burns should be cooled with cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible.
explanation: After cooling, keep the person warm so they don't get too cold, remove jewellery or clothing near the burn unless it is stuck, and cover the burn loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag. Large, deep or facial burns, chemical or electrical burns, and burns in babies and young children need medical help.

myth: Raising a child with two languages causes speech delay.
fact: Learning two languages does not cause language delay. Bilingual children reach language milestones within the normal range, though they may mix languages for a while.
explanation: A child who is not reaching milestones in either language should be assessed like any other child, rather than the delay being blamed on bilingualism.

myth: Raw (unpasteurised) milk is healthier than pasteurised milk.
fact: Pasteurisation kills harmful bacteria such as Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria and Campylobacter while having little effect on milk's nutritional value. Raw milk carries a much higher risk of serious food poisoning.
explanation: Raw milk is promoted as more natural, with claims about enzymes, probiotics and allergy benefits that are not supported by good evidence. Children, pregnant people, older adults and people with weakened immune systems are most at risk of serious illness. Raw milk can also carry bird flu virus from infected dairy herds.

myth: Reading in dim light ruins your eyesight.
fact: Reading in dim light can make your eyes feel tired and strained, but it does not cause permanent damage to your eyes.
explanation: Low light makes the eyes work harder to focus, which can cause temporary discomfort or headaches. Good lighting makes reading more comfortable. Lasting changes in vision should be checked by an optometrist.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Regular exercise can help with depression.
fact: Physical activity can reduce symptoms of mild to moderate depression and is recommended alongside other treatments. It also lowers the risk of developing depression.
explanation: Exercise does not replace professional care for moderate or severe depression, but it is a useful part of treatment and costs little. Even walking counts, and activity that fits your situation is easier to keep up. If you are struggling, talking to a GP, a doctor or a mental health helpline is a good first step.

myth: Regular exercise can lower blood pressure.
fact: Regular physical activity helps lower blood pressure and reduces the risk of heart disease and stroke. Health guidance recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week for adults.
explanation: Some people with high blood pressure worry exercise is unsafe, or doubt it makes a difference. Brisk walking, cycling and swimming all count. If your blood pressure is very high or you have heart symptoms, check with a doctor before starting something strenuous.

myth: Regularly not getting enough sleep is bad for your health.
fact: Ongoing short sleep is linked to higher risks of obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, depression and accidents.
explanation: Adults generally need at least seven hours a night. Occasional poor nights are normal, but if you regularly struggle to sleep or feel exhausted, it is worth speaking to a doctor.

myth: Rub frostbitten fingers or toes with snow to warm them up.
fact: Rubbing frostbitten skin, with snow or anything else, can cause more damage. Frostbitten areas should be warmed gently, for example in warm (not hot) water, and only when there is no risk of them refreezing.
explanation: Don't use direct heat such as a fire or heater, as numb skin burns easily. Frostbite needs medical assessment, and the person may also have hypothermia. Remove wet clothing and keep them warm while getting help.

myth: Rubbing a little whisky or brandy on a baby's gums is a good teething remedy.
fact: Alcohol should never be put on a baby's gums or given to a baby. Babies are very sensitive to alcohol, and even small amounts can be harmful; health guidance specifically says not to rub alcohol on a child's gums.
explanation: This remedy was common in past generations in many countries. Safer options include a clean, chilled teething ring, gently rubbing the gums with a clean finger, and age-appropriate infant painkillers if your baby seems in pain. Avoid aspirin and teething powders.

sources.label: NHS — Tips for helping your teething baby

myth: Rubbing in cocoa butter or special creams prevents stretch marks in pregnancy.
fact: There is no good evidence that creams or oils prevent stretch marks. Whether you get them depends mostly on genetics and how quickly the skin stretches.
explanation: Moisturisers can relieve itchy, dry skin, which may feel helpful. Stretch marks usually fade to a paler colour over time.

myth: Running will wear out your knees and give you arthritis.
fact: Studies of recreational runners have not found that running increases the risk of knee osteoarthritis, and it may even be linked to healthier knees.
explanation: Previous knee injury, excess weight and genetics are bigger risk factors for knee arthritis. Increasing distance gradually and listening to pain helps prevent overuse injuries.

myth: Schizophrenia means having a split or multiple personality.
fact: Schizophrenia is a serious mental illness that can cause psychosis, such as hearing voices or holding false beliefs, along with reduced motivation and difficulties with thinking. It does not involve multiple personalities, which is a different and rare condition.
explanation: The confusion comes from the name, which roughly means 'split mind'. With treatment, including medicine, talking therapy and social support, many people with schizophrenia manage their symptoms and lead fulfilling lives. Early help gives the best outcome.

myth: Severe period pain is always normal and you just have to put up with it.
fact: Mild to moderate period pain is common, but pain that stops you doing daily activities is not something to ignore. It can be a sign of conditions such as endometriosis or adenomyosis.
explanation: Endometriosis often takes years to diagnose partly because severe pain is dismissed as normal. Pain relief, hormonal treatments and other options are available, so see a doctor if pain is severe or getting worse.

myth: Sex, exercise or lifting things in early pregnancy cause miscarriage.
fact: Most miscarriages are caused by chromosome problems in the pregnancy and are not caused by anything the person did. Sex, normal exercise and working do not cause miscarriage.
explanation: Many people blame themselves after a miscarriage, but it is usually not preventable. Smoking, alcohol and some medical conditions do raise the risk. Support is available for anyone affected by pregnancy loss.

myth: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker, darker or faster.
fact: Shaving does not change the thickness, colour or growth rate of hair.
explanation: Shaving cuts hair at a blunt angle, so regrowth can feel coarse, and short new hair may look darker because it has not been lightened by the sun. This has been tested in studies since the 1920s.

myth: Short bursts of activity throughout the day still count towards your exercise.
fact: All physical activity counts. WHO guidance says that any amount of activity is better than none, and activity does not need to be done in long sessions.
explanation: Taking the stairs, brisk walks and active chores add up. Adults are advised to aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus muscle strengthening on two days.

myth: Sitting on cold ground, stone steps or concrete gives you piles.
fact: Piles (haemorrhoids) are linked to constipation and straining on the toilet, pregnancy, heavy lifting, long-lasting coughs and getting older. Sitting on something cold is not a recognised cause.
explanation: This warning is common in many countries, often from parents and grandparents. Sitting on a cold surface may be uncomfortable, but it does not damage the blood vessels in the back passage. Eating enough fibre, drinking fluids and not straining are the best ways to prevent piles.

myth: Sitting too close to the TV damages children's eyes.
fact: Sitting close to a TV or screen does not damage the eyes, though it may cause temporary eye strain.
explanation: Children can focus up close more easily than adults, so they often sit near the screen. A child who always sits very close or squints may be short-sighted and should have an eye test.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Skipping breakfast makes you gain weight.
fact: Studies linking breakfast skipping to higher weight are mostly observational, and randomised trials have not shown that eating breakfast helps people lose weight. What matters more is the overall quality and amount of food across the day.
explanation: Breakfast has long been called the most important meal of the day, partly thanks to cereal advertising. Some people find a healthy breakfast helps them avoid unhealthy snacking later, which is a good reason to eat it. Children and teenagers are generally advised to eat breakfast.

myth: Slow breathing exercises can help calm feelings of stress and anxiety.
fact: Health services recommend simple breathing exercises, such as breathing in slowly through the nose and out through the mouth, as a way to ease stress, anxiety and panic in the moment.
explanation: Breathing techniques are a helpful tool, but they are not a cure for an anxiety disorder. If anxiety is frequent or affects daily life, talking therapies and other treatments can help, and a GP is a good first step.

myth: Smoking causes many types of cancer, not just lung cancer.
fact: Tobacco smoking causes cancers of the lung, mouth, throat, oesophagus, bladder, kidney, pancreas, stomach, cervix and others. Tobacco use is the single largest preventable cause of cancer worldwide.
explanation: Many people think smoking risk is limited to the lungs, or that light smoking is safe. There is no safe level of smoking, and second-hand smoke also causes cancer. Stopping at any age lowers risk, and free support to quit is available in many countries.

myth: Snoring is always harmless.
fact: Snoring is common and often harmless, but loud snoring with pauses in breathing, gasping or daytime sleepiness can be a sign of obstructive sleep apnoea, which needs medical attention.
explanation: Untreated sleep apnoea is linked to high blood pressure and accidents from sleepiness. If a partner notices you stop breathing at night, or you are very tired during the day, see a doctor.

myth: Some dog and cat breeds are completely hypoallergenic.
fact: No dog or cat breed is completely free of allergens. The proteins that trigger pet allergy are found in skin flakes, saliva and urine, not just fur, so low-shedding breeds can still cause symptoms.
explanation: Some people do react less to certain individual animals, which fuels the marketing of 'hypoallergenic' breeds. Studies measuring allergen levels in homes have not found consistent differences between so-called hypoallergenic and other breeds. People with pet allergy or asthma may want to spend time with a specific animal before committing to it.

myth: Someone having a severe allergic reaction should stand up or walk around to keep their blood flowing.
fact: During anaphylaxis, blood pressure can drop suddenly, and standing or walking can make this worse. Health services advise lying the person down with their legs raised, or sitting them up if they are struggling to breathe, and not letting them stand up suddenly.
explanation: If the person becomes unconscious, place them on their side in the recovery position, and if they stop breathing start CPR. Always use their adrenaline auto-injector if they have one and call emergency services.

myth: Spending time outdoors helps protect children from becoming short-sighted.
fact: Studies show children who spend more time outdoors are less likely to develop short-sightedness (myopia).
explanation: Bright daylight is thought to be part of the reason. Outdoor time may delay onset more than slow existing myopia. Regular eye tests help catch vision problems early.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Spicy food causes stomach ulcers.
fact: Most stomach ulcers are caused by infection with Helicobacter pylori bacteria or by long-term use of anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen and aspirin. Spicy food does not cause ulcers, though it may worsen symptoms in some people.
explanation: For decades, ulcers were blamed on diet and stress (stress may worsen symptoms but rarely causes ulcers on its own), until research in the 1980s showed the role of H. pylori, which earned a Nobel Prize. Ulcers caused by H. pylori can usually be cured with antibiotics and acid-reducing medicine. Black or bloody stools or vomiting blood need urgent medical attention.

myth: St John's wort is a safe, natural antidepressant you can take with anything.
fact: Some studies suggest St John's wort may help mild to moderate depression, but it interacts with many medicines, including the contraceptive pill, blood thinners, some heart and HIV medicines and other antidepressants, and can make them less effective or cause harmful effects.
explanation: Products also vary in strength. Taking it with prescribed antidepressants can cause a dangerous reaction called serotonin syndrome. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before trying it, and see a GP if low mood lasts more than a couple of weeks.

myth: Starting insulin means you've failed, and insulin causes blindness and amputations.
fact: Diabetes complications such as eye, kidney and nerve damage are caused by high blood sugar over time, not by insulin. Insulin is a natural hormone, and starting it in type 2 diabetes is often simply part of how the condition progresses.
explanation: People sometimes see relatives start insulin late, after complications have already developed, and wrongly link the two. Type 2 diabetes often gets worse over the years as the pancreas makes less insulin, regardless of effort. Good blood sugar control, including with insulin when needed, lowers the risk of complications.

myth: Statins are dangerous and don't really prevent heart attacks.
fact: Statins lower LDL cholesterol and have been shown in many large trials to reduce heart attacks and strokes in people at increased risk. Most people take them without serious side effects.
explanation: Muscle aches are the most commonly reported side effect, but in blinded trials many such aches occurred as often with placebo as with statins. Serious muscle damage is rare. If you have side effects, a doctor can often change the dose or type rather than stopping altogether.

myth: Staying physically active can lower your risk of dementia.
fact: Regular physical activity is linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia, and WHO recommends it as part of reducing dementia risk.
explanation: Much of the evidence comes from observational studies, so exact effects are uncertain, but activity also protects the heart and blood vessels, which supports the brain. It cannot guarantee someone will not get dementia.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Stomach ulcers are caused by stress.
fact: Most stomach ulcers are caused by an infection with Helicobacter pylori bacteria or by long-term use of anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen or aspirin. Stress may worsen symptoms but is not usually the cause.
explanation: Very severe physical stress, such as major burns or critical illness in hospital, can cause a type of ulcer, which may be where the idea started. For everyday ulcers, testing for H. pylori and reviewing painkiller use is the important step, and the infection can be treated with antibiotics. Black, tarry poo or vomiting blood are emergency signs.

sources.label: NIDDK — Peptic ulcers (stomach and duodenal ulcers)

myth: Strength training is good for older adults.
fact: Muscle-strengthening activities help older adults maintain muscle, bone density and balance, and reduce the risk of falls.
explanation: Muscle mass naturally declines with age, and strength training slows this. Resistance bands, body-weight exercises and light weights all count. Starting gradually is sensible.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Stretching before exercise prevents injury.
fact: Research has not shown that static stretching before exercise reliably prevents injuries. A gradual warm-up with light, movement-based activity is generally recommended instead.
explanation: Stretching can improve flexibility over time, which is useful for some sports and for daily movement. Holding long static stretches right before explosive activity may briefly reduce power. Building up training load gradually matters more for injury prevention.

myth: Sugar makes children hyperactive.
fact: Controlled studies, in which neither parents nor children knew whether the child had sugar, have not found that sugar causes hyperactivity. Parents who believed their child had eaten sugar were more likely to rate them as hyperactive.
explanation: Children often get sugary food at parties and celebrations, where excitement levels are already high. Too much sugar is still bad for teeth and can contribute to unhealthy weight gain. Limiting sweets and sugary drinks is good advice, just not for behaviour reasons.

myth: Sugar makes children hyperactive.
fact: Controlled studies have not found that sugar causes hyperactivity in children, including children with ADHD.
explanation: Parents who expect sugar to cause hyperactivity tend to rate their children as more hyperactive. Parties and celebrations are exciting anyway. Limiting sugar is still good for teeth and overall health.

myth: Suicide happens without any warning, so there's nothing anyone can do.
fact: Many people who die by suicide show warning signs beforehand, such as talking about wanting to die or being a burden, withdrawing from others, giving away possessions, or sudden changes in mood or behaviour. Suicide is often preventable, and reaching out can make a difference.
explanation: Not every warning sign is obvious, and people who lose someone to suicide are not to blame. If you are worried about someone, ask them directly and listen without judgement. If you are having thoughts of suicide yourself, please contact a crisis line, a GP or emergency services; you do not have to cope alone.

myth: Sunscreen causes skin cancer.
fact: There is no good evidence that sunscreen causes skin cancer. Regular sunscreen use, together with shade and clothing, helps reduce the risk of skin cancers.
explanation: Some sunscreen ingredients are being studied further by regulators, but health agencies continue to recommend broad-spectrum sunscreen. Mineral sunscreens with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide are an option for people with concerns.

myth: Swallowed chewing gum stays in your stomach for seven years.
fact: Your body cannot digest gum base, but swallowed gum passes through the digestive system and leaves in your stool within days, like other undigestible material.
explanation: This is a classic warning to children. Very rarely, swallowing large amounts of gum, especially with other objects, has caused blockages in young children. Swallowing a piece occasionally is not a concern.

myth: Swallowing fruit seeds, like watermelon or grape seeds, gives you appendicitis or makes a plant grow in your stomach.
fact: Swallowed seeds normally pass through the gut and out in your poo. Nothing can grow in the stomach, and seeds are not a recognised cause of appendicitis; the exact cause of appendicitis is often unclear.
explanation: Appendicitis is thought to happen when the appendix becomes blocked or infected. Its typical sign is tummy pain that starts around the belly button and moves to the lower right side, getting worse over time. That kind of pain needs urgent medical help, whatever someone has eaten.

myth: Sweating a lot in saunas or sweat suits burns fat.
fact: Sweating loses water, not fat. Any weight lost through sweating returns as soon as you rehydrate, and losing too much fluid can be dangerous.
explanation: The scales do show a drop after a sauna or sweaty workout, which makes the belief convincing. Exercising in heavy clothing in hot conditions increases the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke. How much you sweat is not a measure of how much fat you burn.

myth: Taking folic acid before and in early pregnancy helps prevent birth defects.
fact: Folic acid taken before conception and in early pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida.
explanation: The neural tube forms very early, often before people know they are pregnant, so it is recommended that anyone who could become pregnant takes folic acid daily. Some people need a higher dose on medical advice.

myth: Taking ibuprofen makes COVID-19 or viral infections much worse.
fact: Reviews by health authorities found no clear evidence that ibuprofen worsens COVID-19. Ibuprofen and paracetamol can both be used to ease symptoms, following the usual precautions on the label.
explanation: The concern spread widely in early 2020 after comments on social media and some early advice to prefer paracetamol while evidence was reviewed. Ibuprofen is still unsuitable for some people, for example those with certain kidney, stomach or heart problems, or some people with asthma. A pharmacist can advise which painkiller suits you.

myth: Taking laxatives is a good way to lose weight or get rid of calories.
fact: Laxatives act on the large bowel, after most calories have already been absorbed, so they do not stop the body taking in food energy. Any weight lost is water, which returns, and misusing laxatives can cause dehydration, dangerous changes in body salts and long-term bowel problems.
explanation: Using laxatives to control weight can be a sign of an eating disorder. If you, or someone you know, feel you need to use laxatives, vomiting or extreme dieting to manage weight, please talk to a GP or an eating disorder support service; help is available and recovery is possible.

myth: Taking medicine after its expiry date is poisonous.
fact: Most expired medicines do not become toxic, but they may lose strength and the manufacturer no longer guarantees they work or are safe. Some medicines, such as liquid antibiotics, insulin, adrenaline pens and eye drops, should not be used past their date.
explanation: Old reports of tetracycline antibiotics becoming harmful contributed to the fear, but the main risk today is reduced effectiveness. For important medicines, a weaker dose can be dangerous. Return expired medicines to a pharmacy for safe disposal rather than using them.

sources.label: FDA — Don't be tempted to use expired medicines

myth: Taking more vitamins is always better, because extra just gets flushed out.
fact: Some vitamins and minerals are harmful in high doses. Too much vitamin A, vitamin D or iron, for example, can cause serious side effects, and vitamin A in high doses can harm an unborn baby.
explanation: It is true that excess of some water-soluble vitamins is passed in urine, but even these can cause problems at very high doses, such as nerve damage from large amounts of vitamin B6. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) can build up in the body. Check labels and talk to a pharmacist before taking high-dose products.

sources.label: NIH ODS — Vitamin A fact sheet

myth: Taking paracetamol (Tylenol, acetaminophen) during pregnancy causes autism.
fact: Research has not shown that paracetamol in pregnancy causes autism. The WHO has said there is no conclusive evidence of a link and that no consistent association has been established, and paracetamol remains the usual first-choice painkiller in pregnancy.
explanation: Some studies have reported associations, but these can be explained by other factors, such as the illness the medicine was taken for; large studies comparing siblings did not find a link. As with any medicine in pregnancy, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time. High fever in pregnancy carries its own risks, so do not avoid treatment out of fear; ask a midwife, pharmacist or doctor.

myth: Taking the contraceptive pill for years makes you infertile.
fact: The contraceptive pill does not cause long-term infertility. Fertility usually returns quickly after stopping.
explanation: Fertility does decline with age, so people who stop the pill later in life may take longer to conceive, but this is due to age rather than the pill. The contraceptive injection can delay the return of fertility for up to a year.

myth: Taking vitamin C supplements stops you catching colds.
fact: For most people, regular vitamin C supplements do not reduce the chance of catching a cold. They may slightly shorten colds, and people under heavy physical stress, such as marathon runners, may get some protection.
explanation: Vitamin C became famous as a cold remedy in the 1970s, and the idea has stuck. Starting vitamin C after symptoms begin does not appear to help. Most people get enough vitamin C from fruit and vegetables, and very high doses can cause stomach upset.

sources.label: NIH ODS — Vitamin C fact sheet

myth: Talking therapies such as CBT can be an effective treatment for depression and anxiety.
fact: Talking therapies, including cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), are recommended treatments for common mental health problems such as depression and anxiety disorders. For mild to moderate depression they are often offered before, or alongside, medicine.
explanation: Therapy is not 'just chatting': it is a structured treatment that teaches practical ways to manage thoughts, feelings and behaviours. In some areas, such as England, you can refer yourself to NHS talking therapy services without seeing a GP first.

myth: Tanning beds are a safer way to tan than the sun.
fact: Sunbeds give off UV radiation that increases the risk of skin cancer, including melanoma. They are not safer than the sun.
explanation: WHO classifies UV-emitting tanning devices as carcinogenic to humans, and many countries restrict their use by under-18s. Fake tan products are a safer alternative.

myth: Teenagers who sleep late are just lazy.
fact: During adolescence the body clock naturally shifts later, making it harder for teenagers to fall asleep early and wake early. Teens also need around eight to ten hours of sleep.
explanation: Early school starts combined with a later body clock leave many teenagers short of sleep, which affects mood and learning. Regular sleep times and limiting late-night screens can help.

myth: Teething causes a high fever in babies.
fact: Teething may cause a slightly raised temperature, but it does not cause a high fever. A high temperature in a baby should be assessed for another cause.
explanation: Teething can cause sore gums, drooling and fussiness. Babies under three months with a temperature of 38C or more, or any baby who seems very unwell, need urgent medical advice.

myth: Teething causes diarrhoea and nappy rash.
fact: Teething can cause sore gums, dribbling, chewing and some fussiness, but there is little evidence that it causes diarrhoea. Diarrhoea in a teething baby is more likely to have another cause, such as a tummy bug.
explanation: Teething happens over many months at the same age that babies start putting everything in their mouths and catching common infections, so the two often overlap. Blaming teething can mean missing signs of illness. Babies with diarrhoea can become dehydrated quickly; seek advice if they have fewer wet nappies, are drowsy or are not feeding.

myth: Testicular cancer only affects older men.
fact: Testicular cancer is most common in younger men, roughly between 15 and 49 years old.
explanation: It is one of the most treatable cancers, especially when found early. A painless lump, swelling or change in a testicle should be checked by a doctor.

myth: The best way to remove a tick is to burn it with a match or smother it with Vaseline or nail polish.
fact: Ticks should be removed as soon as possible with fine-tipped tweezers or a tick-removal tool, grasping the tick close to the skin and pulling upwards slowly and steadily. Afterwards, clean the bite and wash your hands.
explanation: Burning or smothering a tick takes time and may cause it to release more fluid into the bite, which could raise the risk of infections such as Lyme disease. Watch the area for a spreading circular red rash or flu-like symptoms over the following weeks and see a doctor if they appear.

myth: The Chinese gender calendar can predict or help you choose your baby's sex.
fact: There is no evidence that a chart based on the mother's age and the month of conception can predict or influence a baby's sex. Whether a baby is a boy or a girl depends on whether the sperm that fertilises the egg carries an X or a Y chromosome.
explanation: Because there are only two likely outcomes, the calendar will be 'right' about half the time, which makes it feel accurate. Studies that checked such charts against real births found they did no better than chance. A scan in mid-pregnancy is the usual way to find out.

myth: The flu jab gives you the flu.
fact: Injected flu vaccines contain inactivated virus or a single viral protein and cannot cause flu. Some people get a sore arm, mild temperature or aches for a day or two, which is the immune system responding, not flu.
explanation: The myth persists because flu vaccines are given in autumn, when colds and other viruses are circulating, so some people catch an unrelated bug soon after. Protection also takes about two weeks to develop. The children's nasal spray contains weakened live virus that is designed not to cause flu illness.

myth: The HPV vaccine encourages teenagers to have sex earlier.
fact: Studies have found that HPV vaccination does not lead to earlier or riskier sexual activity. The vaccine is given before people are likely to be exposed to HPV because it works best then.
explanation: Because HPV spreads through sexual contact, some parents worry that vaccinating implies approval of sex. The vaccine is about preventing cancers later in life, including cervical, throat and anal cancers. Countries with high HPV vaccine coverage have seen large drops in HPV infections and in cervical pre-cancers.

myth: The HPV vaccine helps prevent cervical cancer.
fact: Almost all cervical cancers are caused by persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV). The HPV vaccine protects against the types that cause most cervical cancers, and countries with high coverage have seen big falls in cervical pre-cancers and cancers.
explanation: Some people doubt that a vaccine can prevent cancer. HPV vaccination also protects against other HPV-related cancers, such as some throat, anal and genital cancers. Vaccinated people should still attend cervical screening when invited, because the vaccine does not cover every HPV type.

myth: The keto diet is the best and only diet that really works for weight loss.
fact: A very low-carbohydrate (ketogenic) diet can lead to weight loss, mainly because it reduces how much people eat. Over the longer term, studies find it does not beat other approaches that cut calories by a similar amount, and many people find it hard to stick to.
explanation: Early weight loss on keto is partly water, because the body's carbohydrate stores hold water. Strict keto cuts out many fruits, whole grains and pulses that provide fibre, and it can cause side effects such as constipation; it may not be suitable for people with some medical conditions or on certain medicines. The diet that works best for any one person is usually the one they can keep up while still eating a balanced range of foods.

sources.label: Harvard Health Publishing — Should you try the keto diet?

myth: The MMR vaccine causes autism.
fact: Large studies involving millions of children in several countries have found no link between the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine and autism. The 1998 paper that started the claim was retracted and its lead author was struck off the UK medical register.
explanation: The fear spread because autism signs often become noticeable around the same age that children receive the MMR jab, so the timing can look connected. Falling vaccination rates after the scare led to measles outbreaks, and measles can cause pneumonia, brain swelling and death. Delaying or splitting the vaccine leaves children unprotected for longer without any benefit.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: The more you sweat, the more fat you burn.
fact: Sweating is how the body cools down; it is not a measure of fat burned. Weight lost through sweat is water that returns when you drink.
explanation: How much you sweat depends on temperature, humidity, fitness and genetics. Sweat suits or exercising in heat to lose weight can cause dehydration and heat illness.

myth: The pull-out method is a reliable way to avoid pregnancy.
fact: Withdrawal is one of the least reliable methods of contraception because pre-ejaculate can contain sperm and timing is difficult in practice.
explanation: With typical use, many couples relying on withdrawal will have an unplanned pregnancy within a year. It also gives no protection against sexually transmitted infections.

myth: Therapy is only for people who are seriously mentally ill.
fact: Talking therapies help with a wide range of problems, including stress, anxiety, low mood, grief and relationship difficulties. You do not need a serious diagnosis to benefit.
explanation: Approaches such as cognitive behavioural therapy have strong evidence for common problems. Many health services let people refer themselves for talking therapy.

myth: There is no known safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy.
fact: Health authorities advise not drinking at all during pregnancy because no safe level of alcohol has been established.
explanation: Alcohol passes to the baby and can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders. If you drank before you knew you were pregnant, the risk of harm is likely to be low; talk to your midwife or doctor if you are worried.

myth: Tilt your head back to stop a nosebleed.
fact: For a nosebleed, sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of your nose just above the nostrils for 10 to 15 minutes. Tilting the head back makes blood run down the throat, which can cause choking or vomiting.
explanation: Tilting back seems to stop the bleeding because the blood is no longer visible, but it is still flowing. Breathe through your mouth while pinching. Get urgent help if a nosebleed lasts more than 10 to 15 minutes despite pressure, follows a head injury, or is very heavy.

myth: To get pregnant you only need to have sex on the day you ovulate, and ovulation always happens on day 14.
fact: The fertile window covers several days before ovulation as well as the day itself, because sperm can survive for up to about 5 days. Ovulation does not always happen on day 14; it varies between people and from cycle to cycle.
explanation: Trying to time sex to one exact day can add stress and miss the best days. Health services suggest having sex every two to three days throughout the cycle. Ovulation kits and apps can help some people, but they are not essential.

myth: Touching or washing a baby's soft spot can damage their brain.
fact: A baby's soft spots (fontanelles) are covered by a tough membrane that protects the brain. Gently touching them, washing the head or brushing the hair will not cause harm.
explanation: The soft spots let the skull grow with the brain and close over the first couple of years. A soft spot that looks sunken can be a sign of dehydration, and one that is bulging while the baby is calm can be a sign of a serious problem, so seek medical advice urgently if you notice either.

myth: Turmeric or curcumin cures inflammation, arthritis and cancer.
fact: There is no convincing evidence that turmeric or curcumin cures any disease. Curcumin is poorly absorbed by the body, and research results for conditions like arthritis have been limited and mixed.
explanation: Turmeric has a long history in traditional medicine and lab studies of curcumin are often promoted online. High-dose turmeric supplements have been linked to cases of liver injury. Using turmeric in cooking is safe for most people.

myth: Type 1 diabetes can be cured with diet or herbs, so insulin can be stopped.
fact: People with type 1 diabetes cannot make enough insulin and need it to survive. Stopping insulin can cause diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening emergency, within hours to days.
explanation: Some online sellers and practitioners claim diets or herbal products can replace insulin, and there have been deaths after people followed this advice. Research into cures, such as islet cell transplants, is ongoing but these are not widely available. Signs of ketoacidosis include vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing and confusion and need emergency care.

myth: Type 1 diabetes is caused by eating too many sweets as a child.
fact: Type 1 diabetes happens when the immune system destroys the insulin-making cells in the pancreas. It is not caused by diet or lifestyle and cannot currently be prevented.
explanation: Confusion between type 1 and type 2 diabetes leads to blame being placed on children and parents. The exact triggers are not fully known, but genetics and possibly viral infections are thought to play a role. Type 1 diabetes always needs insulin.

myth: Type 2 diabetes can sometimes go into remission with weight loss.
fact: Research shows that substantial weight loss, especially soon after diagnosis, can bring blood sugar back to a non-diabetic range without medication in some people with type 2 diabetes. This is called remission rather than a cure, because diabetes can return if weight is regained.
explanation: Many people believe type 2 diabetes is always permanent and progressive. Remission is more likely in people diagnosed recently who lose a significant amount of weight, but it is not possible for everyone. Any major diet change, such as a very low-calorie programme, should be done with medical support because medicines may need adjusting.

myth: Type 2 diabetes is a mild form of diabetes and not serious.
fact: Type 2 diabetes is a serious condition that, if poorly controlled, can lead to heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, sight loss and amputations. It is a leading cause of these complications worldwide.
explanation: Because it often develops slowly and may be managed with tablets or diet at first, people sometimes describe it as 'a touch of sugar'. Many people have no symptoms for years while damage builds up. Regular checks of blood sugar, blood pressure, cholesterol, eyes, kidneys and feet help prevent complications.

myth: Ultrasound scans in pregnancy can harm the baby.
fact: Ultrasound uses sound waves, not radiation, and there are no known risks to the baby or mother from routine pregnancy scans. They are used to check the baby's development and to look for some health conditions.
explanation: Health services recommend scans done for medical reasons by trained staff. Some professional bodies discourage 'keepsake' scans that are long or repeated without a medical purpose, as a precaution. Ask your midwife if you have questions about what a scan can show.

myth: Untreated hearing loss is linked to a higher risk of dementia.
fact: Hearing loss in midlife is among the potentially modifiable risk factors linked to dementia, and treating it may help reduce risk.
explanation: Researchers are still working out whether hearing aids directly lower dementia risk. Hearing loss can lead to social isolation and extra mental effort, which may play a role. Having hearing checked is worthwhile in any case.

sources.label: National Institute on Aging — Health information

myth: Using a decongestant nasal spray for weeks can make your blocked nose worse.
fact: Decongestant nasal sprays should only be used for a short time, usually no more than 5 to 7 days. Using them for longer can cause rebound congestion, where the nose becomes more blocked when the spray wears off.
explanation: This is different from steroid nasal sprays, which are designed for longer-term use in conditions such as hay fever. If you find you can't stop using a decongestant spray, a pharmacist or GP can advise on how to come off it and on treating the underlying cause.

myth: Using computers and phones permanently damages your eyes.
fact: Screen use can cause digital eye strain, with tired, dry or sore eyes and blurred vision, but there is no evidence it causes permanent eye damage in adults.
explanation: We blink less when focusing on screens, which dries the eyes. Taking regular breaks, such as looking about 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes, can help. Lots of close work and little time outdoors may play a role in childhood short-sightedness.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Using mouthwash is as good as brushing your teeth.
fact: Mouthwash cannot replace brushing and cleaning between teeth because it does not remove plaque stuck to the teeth.
explanation: Some mouthwashes contain fluoride or antibacterial agents that can be a useful extra. Persistent bad breath may have an underlying cause worth checking with a dentist.

myth: Using phones and screens in bed can make it harder to sleep.
fact: Using screens before bed is linked to later bedtimes and poorer sleep, partly because content keeps the brain alert and bright light can delay the body clock.
explanation: The effect of screen light alone may be smaller than often claimed; the stimulating content and lost sleep time matter too. Putting devices away for a while before bed is a common recommendation.

myth: Using tampons means you lose your virginity.
fact: Using a tampon has nothing to do with virginity, which is a social idea about sexual activity, not a physical state that a tampon can change.
explanation: The hymen naturally varies and often has an opening; it can stretch with everyday activities. Tampons are safe for most people from their first period, as long as they are changed regularly to reduce the rare risk of toxic shock syndrome.

myth: Vaccines are full of toxic mercury and aluminium.
fact: The amounts of any such ingredients in vaccines are very small and are not harmful. Thiomersal, a mercury-based preservative, has been removed from or reduced to trace amounts in routine childhood vaccines in many countries, and aluminium salts are used in tiny amounts to strengthen the immune response.
explanation: Words like mercury and aluminium sound alarming, but the dose is what matters. Babies take in more aluminium from food and breast milk or formula over their first months than from vaccines. The type of mercury once used in thiomersal (ethylmercury) is cleared from the body faster than the methylmercury found in some fish.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: Vaccines are rushed out without proper safety testing.
fact: Vaccines go through laboratory studies and several phases of clinical trials before licensing, and their safety is monitored continuously afterwards through reporting systems. Rare side effects found after approval have led to changes in advice, which shows the monitoring works.
explanation: COVID-19 vaccines were developed quickly, which made many people uneasy. The speed came from earlier research on similar viruses, large funding, running trial phases in parallel and fast regulatory review, not from skipping steps. Like all medicines, vaccines can have side effects, and these are published openly.

myth: Vaccines cause sudden infant death syndrome (cot death).
fact: Studies have not found that vaccines cause sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Babies are vaccinated in the same months when SIDS is most common, so some deaths will happen after vaccination by coincidence.
explanation: Losing a baby is devastating and families naturally look for a cause. Known ways to lower SIDS risk include placing babies on their back to sleep, keeping the cot clear and avoiding smoke exposure. Some research suggests vaccinated babies are not at higher risk of SIDS than unvaccinated babies.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: Vaccines contain microchips used to track people.
fact: Vaccines do not contain microchips, tracking devices or any electronics. Their ingredients are listed publicly and consist of the active component plus small amounts of stabilisers, salts and sometimes adjuvants.
explanation: This claim spread widely during the COVID-19 pandemic, often mixed with conspiracy theories about governments or billionaires. A working tracking chip would need a power source and antenna and could not pass through a standard vaccine needle. Ingredient lists for licensed vaccines are published by regulators and manufacturers.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: Vaccines weaken your immune system.
fact: Vaccines train your immune system to recognise specific pathogens. They strengthen your body’s defences rather than weakening them, and are among the most studied medical interventions in history.
explanation: Vaccines contain weakened, inactivated or partial pieces of a germ, or instructions to make a harmless piece, that teach the immune system to respond quickly. Mild side effects like a sore arm or brief fever are signs the immune system is responding, not being damaged.

myth: Vaginal douching or special washes keep the vagina clean and healthy.
fact: The vagina cleans itself. Douching and perfumed washes can upset its natural balance and increase the risk of infections such as bacterial vaginosis.
explanation: Washing the outside area (vulva) with water or a mild unperfumed soap is enough. Changes in discharge, smell or itching are worth checking with a doctor or sexual health clinic.

myth: Vitamin B12 injections give everyone an energy boost.
fact: Vitamin B12 injections treat B12 deficiency, which can cause tiredness and anaemia. In people with normal B12 levels, extra B12 has not been shown to increase energy.
explanation: B12 shots are sold at clinics and wellness centres as energy or weight-loss boosters. People at risk of deficiency include those with pernicious anaemia, older adults, vegans, and people taking certain medicines such as metformin. A blood test can show whether you need treatment.

sources.label: NIH ODS — Vitamin B12 fact sheet

myth: Waking a sleepwalker can harm them or give them a heart attack.
fact: Waking a sleepwalker is not dangerous, although they may be confused or startled. It is usually best to guide them gently back to bed.
explanation: The bigger risk is injury while sleepwalking, such as falls or wandering outside. Securing doors and windows and removing hazards helps. Frequent episodes or risky behaviour are worth discussing with a doctor.

myth: Washing your hands with soap and water prevents infections.
fact: Handwashing with soap and water is one of the most effective ways to prevent the spread of many infections, including diarrhoeal illnesses and respiratory infections such as colds and flu.
explanation: Some people doubt that something so simple makes a real difference. Soap helps lift germs off the skin so they rinse away, and washing for about 20 seconds covers all parts of the hands. Key times are after using the toilet, before eating or preparing food, and after coughing, sneezing or blowing your nose.

myth: We don't need vaccines anymore because these diseases have disappeared.
fact: Most vaccine-preventable diseases still circulate somewhere in the world and return quickly when vaccination rates fall. Measles outbreaks in recent years have occurred in many countries where coverage dropped.
explanation: Diseases like polio and diphtheria seem distant precisely because vaccines have kept them rare. Travel means an infection can arrive from anywhere within a day. Smallpox is the only human disease that has been fully eradicated, and only through vaccination.

sources.label: WHO — Vaccines and immunization: what is vaccination?

myth: We only use 10% of our brains.
fact: Brain imaging shows that we use virtually all of our brain, though not every area is active at the same moment. Even simple tasks involve many regions.
explanation: The myth has no clear scientific origin and is popular in films and self-help marketing. Damage to almost any part of the brain causes some effect, which would not happen if most of it were unused.

myth: Wearing an underwire bra causes breast cancer.
fact: There is no evidence that wearing a bra, underwired or not, causes breast cancer. A large study found no link between bra wearing and breast cancer risk.
explanation: The claim suggests bras block lymph drainage and trap toxins, but this is not how breast cancer develops. Known risk factors include age, inherited genes, alcohol, excess weight after menopause and some hormone treatments. Wear whatever bra is comfortable.

sources.label: National Cancer Institute — Common cancer myths and misconceptions

myth: Wearing glasses makes your eyes weaker and dependent on them.
fact: Glasses correct blurry vision but do not weaken the eyes or make the underlying condition worse.
explanation: Vision can change over time with age or as children grow, which people sometimes blame on their glasses. In children, not wearing prescribed glasses can actually harm visual development in some conditions, such as lazy eye.

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology — Eye health

myth: Wearing hats makes you go bald.
fact: Wearing ordinary hats does not cause hair loss. The most common cause of baldness is inherited male- or female-pattern hair loss.
explanation: Very tight hairstyles or headwear worn constantly can pull on hair and cause traction alopecia, but a normal-fitting cap does not.

myth: Wearing tight underwear makes men infertile.
fact: Tight underwear does not make men infertile. Some research suggests looser underwear may be linked to slightly better sperm measures, because testicles work best a little cooler than body temperature.
explanation: Any effect appears small. Smoking, heavy drinking, obesity and some medicines have clearer effects on sperm. Men having trouble conceiving with a partner can ask a doctor for a semen test.

myth: Weight loss surgery is the easy way out.
fact: Weight loss (bariatric) surgery is a major treatment offered to people with severe obesity, usually after other approaches have been tried. It requires lifelong changes to eating, regular follow-up and often vitamin supplements.
explanation: Surgery can lead to large, lasting weight loss and can improve or even put conditions such as type 2 diabetes into remission. It also carries risks, and people need to adjust how much and how they eat for the rest of their lives. Calling it 'easy' adds stigma and can put people off a treatment that might help them.

myth: Weight-bearing exercise helps keep your bones strong.
fact: Weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise helps build bone in young people and slows bone loss in adults.
explanation: Examples include walking, dancing, jogging, stair climbing and resistance exercises. People with osteoporosis can still exercise but may need advice on safe movements.

myth: When you have diarrhoea you should stop eating, or eat only plain toast and bananas.
fact: The most important thing with diarrhoea is to keep drinking fluids to avoid dehydration. You can eat as soon as you feel able to, and there is no need to stick to a special bland diet.
explanation: Starving yourself does not make diarrhoea stop sooner. Oral rehydration sachets from a pharmacy can help people at risk of dehydration, such as older people and young children. Babies should keep breastfeeding or having formula. Signs of severe dehydration, blood in diarrhoea, or symptoms lasting more than a week need medical advice.

myth: When you're pregnant you need to eat for two.
fact: Most people do not need extra calories in the first six months of pregnancy, and only a modest amount extra later on.
explanation: Eating much more than needed can lead to excess weight gain, which raises the risk of complications such as gestational diabetes. The focus should be on a balanced diet and recommended supplements.

myth: White teeth are healthy teeth.
fact: Tooth colour is not a reliable sign of dental health. Teeth naturally vary in shade, and white teeth can still have decay or gum disease.
explanation: Teeth can also darken with age, food, drinks and smoking. Whitening is cosmetic and is best done with dental advice.
